## 1 From Multivariate Time Series to Anomaly Routing

Analyzing multivariate time series from physical and industrial systems requires distinguishing true operational faults from routine dynamic shifts across multiple coupled sensors. Turning raw sensor streams into actionable diagnostics faces two fundamental hurdles: 

- **Geometric complexity**: as variables interact nonlinearly across shifting operating regimes
- **Computational scalability**: where calibrating alert thresholds, clustering fault modes, and routing live telemetry must execute rapidly across tens of thousands of time points. 

`isoRouting` addresses both challenges within a unified S4 pipeline, bridging non-parametric anomaly isolation with fast, scale-free clustering, fault archetypes, threshold diagnostics and streaming fault triage.

### 1.1 Need for Handling Complex Variable Dependencies

Building predictive diagnostic models for multivariate time series begins with feature selection. A standard machine learning reflex is to compute a linear correlation matrix to identify and drop redundant variables. While useful for simple stochastic processes, this linear assumption frequently breaks down in physical domains.

In industrial Internet of Things (IoT) environments, for example, variables are governed by causal, closed-loop mechanics. To illustrate this, we load the `hvac_features` dataset (Turin HVAC telemetry [@borda2022development]) provided with `isoRouting` and examine the linear correlation across its 10 telemetry channels over time (`timestamp`)


```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Loading Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(isoRouting)

# Load the bundled package data
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")

# Restrict to raw variables (the package data also contains engineered features)
hvac_raw <- hvac_features |>
  select(
    t_supply, t_return, sp_return, t_saturation, t_outdoor,
    rh_supply, rh_return, rh_outdoor, energy, power
  )

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlation
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| code-summary: "Correlation Heatmap Code"
#| fig-cap: "Global Pearson correlation heatmap (Turin HVAC Raw Telemetry)"

library(ggcorrplot)

# Calculate correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(hvac_raw, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# Set the diagonal to NA to de-emphasize trivial self-correlations
diag(cor_matrix) <- NA

# Generate the square ggplot-based heatmap
ggcorrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  method = "square",
  type = "full",
  lab = TRUE,              
  lab_size = 3.0,
  tl.cex = 11,
  lab_col = "black",      
  colors = c("#f8766d", "white", "#00bfc4"),
  outline.color = "gray90",
  legend.title = "Correlation"
) +
theme(
  axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1),
  axis.text.y = element_text()
) +
scale_y_discrete(limits = rev)
```

Based on the heatmap one could be tempted to remove some variables with high correlation. However, examining the raw pairwise dependencies reveals a much more complex geometric reality.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pairs-plot
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Scatterplot Code"
#| dev: "jpeg"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Scatterplot matrix with correlation-mapped backgrounds (Sampled at n = 2,500)"

library(GGally)

# 1. Custom function to calculate correlation and map it to a background color
custom_scatter_bg <- function(data, mapping, ...) {
  x_data <- GGally::eval_data_col(data, mapping$x)
  y_data <- GGally::eval_data_col(data, mapping$y)
 
  corr <- cor(x_data, y_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
 
  color_fun <- colorRamp(c("#f8766d", "white", "#00bfc4"))
  scaled_corr <- (corr + 1) / 2
 
  rgb_vec <- color_fun(scaled_corr)
  hex_color <- rgb(rgb_vec[1], rgb_vec[2], rgb_vec[3], maxColorValue = 255)
 
  ggplot(data, mapping) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
             fill = hex_color, alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(...)
}

# 2. Generate the plot for a sample using the restricted raw data
set.seed(42)
p_pairs <- hvac_raw |>
  sample_n(2000) |>
  ggpairs(
    lower = list(continuous = wrap(custom_scatter_bg, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5)),
    upper = list(continuous = wrap(custom_scatter_bg, alpha = 0.1, size = 0.5)),
    title = "Pairwise Scatterplot Matrix (Raw Telemetry)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA)
  )

p_pairs
```

The scatterplot matrix shows that linear correlation is an inadequate measure here: variables form nonlinear clusters, distinct operating modes, and hard boundaries dictated by mechanical limits and programmed setpoints. Explicitly modeling these dependencies with parametric methods would require a prohibitive expansion of interaction terms.

This geometric complexity is why `isoRouting` builds upon the **Isolation Forest** algorithm [@liu2008isolation]. Rather than modeling the intricate structure of normal operations, an Isolation Forest uses recursive random partitioning to isolate observations that fall outside dense operational regions.

### 1.2 Why `isoRouting`? Fast Calibration, Fault Archetypes, and Streaming Triage

While a standard Isolation Forest assigns an anomaly score $S(x) \in (0, 1)$ to every timestamp, a raw score vector leaves several operational questions unanswered:

- **Feature Selection & Attribution:** *Which engineered features actively drive anomaly isolation, and which ones dilute the upper tail of anomaly scores?*
- **Threshold Calibration:** *Where should we set the anomaly score cutoff?*
- **Fault Mode Discovery & $k$-Selection:** *What distinct physical fault types, called archetypes, exist inside the anomalous tail, and how many clusters ($k$) are structurally stable?*
- **Streaming Triage & Novelty Rejection:** *When new telemetry arrives, does an anomaly match a known historical archetype, or is it a novel failure mode?*
- **Novelty Sub-Clustering:** *Among newly flagged unknown anomalies, are we seeing isolated spikes or distinct emerging archetypes?*

`isoRouting` uses **the fitted Isolation Forest itself** as both the anomaly detector and the similarity engine—extracting terminal leaf memberships directly from the trees to keep every stage of exploration, clustering, and live routing fast:

- **Fast Scoring & Feature Auditing:** Because each tree in an Isolation Forest (`isotree`) is grown on a small, fixed random subsample of observations (`sample_size`, $\psi = 256$) rather than the full time series of length $N$, tree construction scales as $\mathcal{O}(n_t \psi \log \psi)$ (where $n_t$ is the number of trees) and scoring scales linearly as $\mathcal{O}(N n_t \log \psi)$. This allows users to rapidly audit candidate feature sets via permutation or leave-one-out tail attribution without computational bottlenecks.
- **Objective Threshold Calibration ($D$ and $\text{LID}$):** Rather than guessing a score cutoff, users can sweep candidate thresholds to rapidly generate diagnostic profiles for the resulting subset of $N_a$ threshold-induced anomalies ($N_a \ll N$):
  - **Hartigan's Dip Statistic ($D$)** [@hartigan1985dip] tests pairwise tail distances for multimodality, indicating when the tail separates into distinct fault clusters.
  - **Local Intrinsic Dimensionality ($\text{LID}$)** [@amsaleg2015estimating; @houle2017local] estimates the local degrees of freedom via $k$-nearest neighbor distances, identifying when anomalies collapse onto constrained mechanical trajectories ($\text{LID} \ll p$, where $p$ is the number of features) rather than diffuse background noise.
  - Both measures are minimally sensitive to subset size $N_a$ (e.g., $D$ is a scale-free effect size), and their computational speed makes it practical to benchmark observed values against Monte Carlo null distributions.
- **Scale-Free Clustering & Fault Archetypes (`compute_distances`):** Instead of comparing raw sensors with incompatible units, `isoRouting` extracts the $N_a \times n_t$ matrix of terminal leaf IDs from the forest and computes pairwise **Hamming distances** (the fraction of trees in which two points land in different leaves). Partitioning this scale-free distance matrix via divisive hierarchical clustering (**DIANA** [@kaufman1990finding]) splits broad anomalies into specific fault regimes and summarizes each cluster by its **medoid**—an actual historical observation that serves as the cluster's representative **archetype**.
- **Fast Streaming Triage & Novelty Detection (`stream_telemetry`):** Incoming anomalies ($N_{\text{new}}$) are routed by comparing their leaf memberships solely against the $k$ cluster medoids in $\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{new}} k n_t)$ time. Points falling within a cluster's calibrated radius are labeled with that known archetype; points outside all $k$ radii are flagged as **novel anomalies** for further inspection and can be sub-clustered into emerging archetypes when warranted.

@tbl-complexity summarizes the asymptotic time complexity across each stage of the `isoRouting` pipeline.

| Pipeline Stage | S4 Method / Engine Step | Time Complexity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Forest Fit & Scoring** | `ingest_time_course()` / `isotree` | $\mathcal{O}(n_t \psi \log \psi + N n_t \log \psi)$ |
| **Feature Ranking (LOO)** | Leave-one-out tail attribution | $\mathcal{O}(p \cdot N n_t \log \psi)$ |
| **Threshold Controls ($D$, $\text{LID}$)** | `simulate_dip_control()`, `simulate_lid_control()` | $\mathcal{O}(M \cdot N_a \log N_a)$ |
| **Leaf Hamming Distances** | `compute_distances()` | $\mathcal{O}(N_a^2 n_t)$ |
| **Divisive Clustering & Stability** | `evaluate_k_stability()` (DIANA) | $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot k N_a^2)$ |
| **Streaming Triage** | `stream_telemetry()` | $\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{new}} n_t \log \psi + N_{\text{new}} k n_t)$ |

: Computational complexity of the `isoRouting` workflow ($N$: series length; $N_a \ll N$: extracted tail anomalies; $n_t$: number of trees (`isotree`); $\psi$: subsample size (`isotree`); $p$: number of features; $k$: archetype clusters; $M, B$: Monte Carlo/bootstrap iterations; $N_{\text{new}}$: streaming points). {#tbl-complexity}

## 2 Engine Workflow

The `isoRouting` package is built around the `DiagnosticEngine`, a state-based S4 class designed to enforce a sequential workflow. The engine tracks its internal state , ensuring that prerequisites—such as data ingestion, anomaly scoring, and topological distance computation—are completed in the correct order before advanced diagnostic or routing methods can be executed.

### 2.1 Execution Lifecycle

The chronological lifecycle of the `DiagnosticEngine`, from uninitialized configuration to committed forensic ledgers, is outlined in @tbl-engine-workflow.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-engine-workflow
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| code-summary: "Workflow Table Code"

library(knitr)
library(dplyr)

workflow_summary <- data.frame(
  Step = 1:7,
  Method = c(
    "`initialize(config_path)`",
    "`ingest_time_course(data)`",
    "`extract_anomalies(threshold)`",
    "`compute_distances()`",
    "`calibrate(min_k, max_k)`",
    "`extract_medoids(k)`",
    "`commit_ledger()` / `route_time_course()`"
  ),
  Starting_State = c(
    "Uninitialized",
    "Initialized",
    "Time Course Ingested",
    "Anomalies Extracted",
    "Distances Computed",
    "Calibrated",
    "Medoids Extracted"
  ),
  Resulting_State = c(
    "Initialized",
    "Time Course Ingested",
    "Anomalies Extracted",
    "Distances Computed",
    "Calibrated",
    "Medoids Extracted",
    "Ledger Committed"
  ),
  Operational_Purpose = c(
    "Parses the YAML schema, target variables, and machine learning hyperparameters.",
    "Validates timestamps, enforces temporal continuity, and isolates target variables.",
    "Trains the Isolation Forest model, scores the entire time course, and filters extreme events.",
    "Extracts terminal leaf nodes and computes the size-agnostic proportional Hamming distance matrix.",
    "Applies divisive hierarchical clustering (DIANA) across k-values to maximize global silhouette width.",
    "Identifies physical time-series archetypes (medoids) and computes empirical cluster radii (event horizons).",
    "Ranks historical anomalies by distance to medoid, or projects the full time series to track sub-threshold evolution."
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

kable(
  workflow_summary, 
  col.names = c("Step", "Engine Method", "Input State", "Output State", "Operational Purpose"),
  caption = "Chronological execution lifecycle and state transitions of the DiagnosticEngine S4 class."
)
```

## 3 Example of Workflow with Non-Engineered Features

We first illustrate `isoRouting` using a "naive" configuration built strictly on the 10 raw telemetry channels of the Turin HVAC dataset. Omitting dynamic feature engineering will provide a baseline that highlights why encoding temporal rates of change is essential for time-series anomaly routing.

### 3.1 Data Preparation and Temporal Integrity

The first step in the `isoRouting` pipeline is preparing the time-course data. Because the engine's core methods rely on regular time intervals, `DiagnosticEngine` requires a properly formatted datetime column named `timestamp` (`POSIXt`).

We begin by loading the Turin HVAC dataset bundled with the package and verifying the `timestamp` column class:

```{r}
#| label: data-ingestion
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Loading Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(isoRouting)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

# Load the package-associated Turin HVAC dataset
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")

# Verify the timestamp column is present and properly classed
class(hvac_features$timestamp)
```

Before initializing the engine, we scan the dataset for missing periods using `check_time_continuity()`:

```{r}
#| label: continuity-check
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Continuity Check Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Evaluate temporal continuity
continuity_check <- check_time_continuity(hvac_features$timestamp)

# Truncate gap_indices for display while printing the full interval summary
print(modifyList(continuity_check, list(
  gap_indices = c(head(continuity_check$gap_indices, 16), "...")
)))
```

The output of `check_time_continuity()` returns a boolean continuity flag alongside a frequency table of all intervals between consecutive `timestamps`. While the standard polling interval for the Turin HVAC system is 900 seconds (15 minutes), `$summary` reveals a major discontinuity of 15,814,800 seconds (approximately 6 months), alongside several minor outages ranging from a few hours to six days.

Ingesting a 6-month gap would severely distort estimations performed by `isoRouting`. However, the underlying Isolation Forest and distance matrices can handle minor maintenance downtimes without requiring synthetic data imputation.

Therefore, we will split the dataset into two distinct periods across the 6-month boundary. We will use both early and late segments for different purposes in this vignette. We also verify that both segments are continuous within a 7-day tolerance.

<span id="data-split-and-validation" class="flash-target" style="color: #0072B2;">Data Split and Validation</span>
```{r}
#| label: data-split-and-validation
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Split Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Calculate time differences to locate the 6-month gap
time_diffs <- as.numeric(difftime(
  hvac_features$timestamp[-1], 
  hvac_features$timestamp[-nrow(hvac_features)], 
  units = "secs"
))

# Locate the index of the largest gap (6-month shutdown)
major_gap_idx <- which.max(time_diffs)

# Bucket 1: Pre-Gap (~40% of data)
baseline_telemetry <- hvac_features |> 
  slice(1:major_gap_idx)

# Bucket 2: Post-Gap (~60% of data)
stream_telemetry <- hvac_features |> 
  slice((major_gap_idx + 1):n())

# Validate both buckets using a 7-day tolerance (604,800 seconds)
baseline_check <- check_time_continuity(baseline_telemetry$timestamp, 
                                        tolerance = 604800)
stream_check   <- check_time_continuity(stream_telemetry$timestamp, 
                                        tolerance = 604800)

if (!baseline_check$is_continuous || !stream_check$is_continuous) {
  stop("One or both  buckets contain large time discontinuities.")
} else {
  cat(sprintf(
    "Continuity verified (7-day tolerance): Baseline (%d rows) and Stream (%d rows).\n",
    nrow(baseline_telemetry), nrow(stream_telemetry)
  ))
}
```

### 3.2 Engine Configuration and Initialization

The `DiagnosticEngine` uses a YAML configuration file to define its model parameters and feature schema. We start with a naive configuration that passes the raw sensor readings directly to the model.

In `isoRouting`, the schema divides variables into two categories:

- **Target Variables:** Variables used by the Isolation Forest to score anomalies and compute forest-based distances.
- **Context Variables:** Variables excluded from the model, but retained within the extracted medoid time windows for visual interpretation.

In this naive setup, we assign all 10 temperature, humidity, energy, and power channels as target variables and leave the context variables empty. We then instantiate the S4 object with `new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = ...)`.

```{r}
#| label: naive-initialization
#| warning: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Configuration and Instantiation Code"

# Define the naive YAML schema using raw sensor values
yaml_naive <- "
ntrees: 500
sample_size: 256
temporal_window_hours: 2
anomaly_threshold: 0.60
context_variables: []
target_variables:
  - t_supply
  - t_return
  - sp_return
  - t_saturation
  - t_outdoor
  - rh_supply
  - rh_return
  - rh_outdoor
  - energy
  - power
"

# Write the configuration to a temporary file for ingestion
config_naive <- tempfile(pattern = "naive_config_", fileext = ".yml")
writeLines(yaml_naive, config_naive)

# Instantiate the DiagnosticEngine
engine <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_naive)

# Verify the target and context variables parsed from the schema
get_features(engine)
```

### 3.3 Time Course Ingestion

Next, we load the baseline dataset into the S4 object using `ingest_time_course()`. This method verifies that the `timestamp` column is properly formatted and that all `target_variables` from the YAML schema exist in the input data frame. It also drops any columns not listed as target or context variables before storing the validated time course in the engine.

```{r}
#| label: ingest-time-course
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Ingestion Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Ingest the historical baseline telemetry into the engine
engine <- ingest_time_course(engine, data = baseline_telemetry)

# Verify the updated lifecycle state of the engine
engine@domain_state

# Inspect the ingested data structure (features not listed in the YAML are dropped)
glimpse(get_time_course(engine))
```

### 3.4 Anomaly Extraction via Isolation Forest

With the time course ingested, we run `extract_anomalies()` to score the dataset and isolate extreme events.

The `DiagnosticEngine` uses an Isolation Forest (`isotree`) to score the target variables. Rather than relying on geometric distances, Isolation Forests partition the data by randomly selecting a variable and a split value. Because anomalies are rare and distinct, they require fewer splits to isolate, resulting in shorter path lengths in the decision trees and higher anomaly scores (scaled between 0 and 1).

Using the YAML parameters (`ntrees: 500`, `sample_size: 256`), the engine trains the forest, scores the full baseline time course, and stores observations with scores at or above the `0.60` threshold in the `@anomalies` slot.

```{r}
#| label: extract-anomalies
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Anomaly Extraction Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Score the feature space and extract extreme events
engine <- extract_anomalies(engine)

# Verify the engine state
engine@domain_state

# Check how many observations exceeded the 0.60 threshold
nrow(engine@anomalies)
```

### 3.5 Visualizing the Threshold Landscape

In practice, choosing an anomaly threshold does not have to be arbitrary. `isoRouting` provides two quick methods to explore the relationship between the anomaly score threshold ($T$) and the number of extracted events ($N$).

First, `explore_thresholds()` scores the feature space across a sequence of candidate cutoffs without altering the engine's internal state, allowing users to plot the decay curve of isolated events.

```{r}
#| label: naive-explore-thresholds
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Threshold Exploration Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Generate a threshold landscape for the ingested baseline telemetry
threshold_curve <- explore_thresholds(engine, thresholds = seq(0.50, 0.75, by = 0.01))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-threshold-decay
#| def: "jpeg"
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Visualization Code"
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "Anomaly threshold decay curve showing the reduction in isolated extreme events as the Isolation Forest score threshold increases."
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)

# Plot the decay of extreme events
ggplot(threshold_curve, aes(x = Threshold, y = Event_Count)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.60, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Anomaly Threshold Decay Curve",
    subtitle = "Red dashed line indicates the 0.60 YAML selection",
    x = "Isolation Forest Threshold",
    y = "Number of Extracted Events"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )
```

Conversely, get_threshold_at_N() finds the score cutoff required to isolate at least $N$ anomalies.

```{r}
#| label: get-threshold_at_N
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "get_threshold_at_N Call Code"

threshold <- get_threshold_at_N(engine, 40)
cat(paste0("Threshold = ", signif(threshold, 3), " yields at least 40 anomalies\n"))
```

While these two methods map event counts to score cutoffs, they do not indicate whether the isolated events form meaningful clusters. To evaluate how clustering structure changes across thresholds, `isoRouting` provides the `evaluate_k_stability()` diagnostic method presented next.

### 3.6 Threshold Diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: naive-evaluate-stability
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "evaluate_k_stability Call Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Sweep across anomaly counts from N = 800 down to N = 20
stability_curve_naive <- evaluate_k_stability(engine, max_N = 800, min_N = 20, nb_steps = 61, max_k = 10)
```

Method `evaluate_k_stability()` maps the anomaly score threshold ($T$) against three diagnostic metrics. Rather than using Euclidean distances, `isoRouting` computes a proportional Hamming distance: the fraction of trees in the forest where two observations land in different terminal leaves. Because this metric simply counts leaf disagreements, its scale ($0$ to $1$) does not depend on the number of extracted anomalies.

- **Optimal Clusters ($k$)**: At each value of threshold $T$, divisive clustering [@kaufman1990finding] groups the anomalies. The optimal cluster count $k$ (best tree cut) is selected by maximizing the global silhouette score [@rousseeuw1987silhouettes]. Plotting $k$ against $T$ highlights threshold intervals (plateaus) where the cluster partition remains stable.
- **Hartigan's Dip Statistic ($D$)**: Measures the multimodality of all pairwise Hamming distances [@hartigan1985dip]. High values of $D$ indicate strong distance heterogeneity—suggesting distances within clusters are likely smaller than distances between clusters.
- **Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)**: Estimates the number of independent variables governing the isolated points [@amsaleg2015estimating]. A drop in LID suggests a system "breakdown," where variables become more coupled due to a physical fault (e.g. a failed sensor freezing at a constant value reduces the effective degrees of freedom).

<span id="stability-ggplot-target" class="flash-target" style="color: #0072B2;">Diagnostics Plotting Wrapper</span>
```{r}
#| label: stability-ggplot-function
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Ggplot Function Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Define a reusable plotting wrapper
plot_topological_stability <- function(stability_df, plot_title, plot_subtitle) {
  
  # Pivot the profile dataframe for multi-panel plotting
  plot_data <- stability_df |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = c(N_Anomalies, Opt_k, Hartigans_D, Global_LID), 
      names_to = "Metric", 
      values_to = "Value"
    ) |>
    mutate(Metric = factor(Metric, levels = c("N_Anomalies", "Hartigans_D", "Global_LID", "Opt_k")))
  
  # Identify the maximum Hartigan's D for highlighting
  max_dip <- plot_data |>
    filter(Metric == "Hartigans_D") |>
    filter(Value == max(Value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    slice(1)
  
  # Identify the minimum LID for highlighting
  min_lid <- plot_data |>
    filter(Metric == "Global_LID") |>
    filter(Value == min(Value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    slice(1)
  
  # Plot the 4-panel stability profile
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Threshold, y = Value, color = Metric)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_point(data = max_dip, fill = "gold", color = "red", size = 3, shape = 21, stroke = 1.2) +
    geom_point(data = min_lid, fill = "gold", color = "red", size = 3, shape = 21, stroke = 1.2) +
    facet_wrap(
      ~Metric, 
      scales = "free_y", 
      ncol = 1,
      labeller = as_labeller(c(
        N_Anomalies = "Number of Anomalies (N)",
        Hartigans_D = "Cluster Effect Size (Hartigan's Dip Statistic)", 
        Global_LID = "Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)",
        Opt_k = "Optimal Clusters (k)"
      ))
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
      "N_Anomalies" = "#0072B2", 
      "Hartigans_D" = "#009E73", 
      "Global_LID" = "#CC79A7", 
      "Opt_k" = "#D55E00"
    )) +
    scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 10) +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Anomaly Threshold",
      y = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), 
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9),
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
    )
  
  return(p)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-evaluate-stability
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Call Code"
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic profiles across anomaly thresholds using raw telemetry features. Red-bordered gold circles mark the maximum Hartigan's D and minimum LID."
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-width: 7
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Generate the Naive Plot
fig_naive <- plot_topological_stability(
  stability_curve_naive,
  plot_title = "Anomaly Threshold Diagnostics: Naive Configuration",
  plot_subtitle = "Mapping cluster plateaus (k), distance heterogeneity (D), and variable coupling (LID) across thresholds."
)

print(fig_naive)
```

In @fig-naive-evaluate-stability, the optimal cluster count $k$ fluctuates heavily at lower thresholds before settling into a broad plateau at $k = 4$ ($T \in [0.644, 0.662]$) and a final small plateau at $k = 2$ ($T \ge 0.664$). Across the $k = 4$ plateau, Hartigan's $D$ begins to climb while LID drops steadily. Both metrics reach their extremes in the $k = 2$ region: LID hits its minimum ($\approx 3.15$) at $T \approx 0.664$, and $D$ reaches its maximum ($\approx 0.128$) at $T \approx 0.667$.  

To verify whether these $D$ and LID values differ significantly from normal operating variations, we compare them against Monte Carlo control distributions [@phipson2010permutation] generated by `isoRouting` helper functions `simulate_dip_control()` and `simulate_lid_control()`. 

```{r}
#| label: naive-anomaly-thresholds
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Control Dip Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

n_sequence <- seq(20, 100, by = 20)
dip_control_naive <- simulate_dip_control(engine, N = n_sequence, iterations = 100)
```

```{r}
#| label: ggplot-null-dip
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Ggplot Function Code"

library(ggplot2)

# Define a reusable plotting wrapper for all null profiles
plot_baseline_profile <- function(results_df, line_color, plot_title, plot_subtitle, y_label) {
  ggplot(results_df, aes(x = Threshold)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q05, ymax = Q95), fill = line_color, alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_line(aes(y = Median), color = line_color, linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_point(aes(y = Median), color = line_color, size = 3) +
    scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 10) +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Anomaly Threshold",
      y = y_label
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-control-dip
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Call Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Simulated control bounds for Hartigan's Dip Statistic (D). The irregular spacing on the x-axis reflects evaluating the threshold at discrete anomaly counts (N = 20 to 100)."

# Generate the Naive Dip Plot
fig_dip_null_naive <- plot_baseline_profile(
  dip_control_naive,
  line_color = "#009E73", 
  plot_title = "Control Quantiles for Hartigan's D (Naive Configuration)",
  plot_subtitle = "Median and [5%, 95%] bounds estimated with Monte Carlo simulations.",
  y_label = "Hartigan's D"
)

print(fig_dip_null_naive)
```

For each sample size $N \in [20, 100]$, `simulate_dip_control()` uniformly samples $N$ observations from the full ingested time course, builds an Isolation Forest Hamming distance matrix, and computes Hartigan's $D$ across 200 iterations. Because random samples are dominated by normal operations, this preserves the natural variable dependencies of the system. This also provides a conservative baseline for expected distance heterogeneity, by potentially incorporating some of the selected anomalies. 


Comparing @fig-naive-evaluate-stability and @fig-naive-control-dip shows that for $T > 0.651$ ($N \le 100$), the observed $D$ rises from $0.05$ to $0.128$, whereas the 95th percentile of the control distribution remains below $0.044$ across most of the sweep and reaches at most $0.050$ at $N = 20$. This confirms that the distance separation among the top anomalies is not a mathematical artifact caused by calculating $D$ over pairwise distances, which are inherently interdependent.

```{r}
#| label: naive-null-lid-profile-preparation
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Null LID Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

# Run the LID Monte Carlo simulation across the same n_sequence
lid_results_naive <- simulate_lid_control(engine, N = n_sequence, iterations = 100)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-lid-control
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Call Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Simulated control bounds for Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)."

fig_lid_naive <- plot_baseline_profile(
  lid_results_naive,
  line_color = "#CC79A7", 
  plot_title = "Control Quantiles for Intrinsic Dimensionality (Naive Configuration)",
  plot_subtitle = "Median and [5%, 95%] bounds estimated with Monte Carlo simulations.",
  y_label = "Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID)"
)

print(fig_lid_naive)
```

@fig-lid-control applies the same Monte Carlo control strategy to LID. While the observed anomaly LID in @fig-naive-evaluate-stability stays between $3.15$ and $5.4$, the 5th percentile of the control distribution in @fig-lid-control never drops below $8.0$ (with median values between $9.8$ and $12.8$). This confirms that the isolated anomalies exhibit strong variable coupling—i.e., a loss of variability—compared to normal system states.

### 3.7 Archetypes Extractions

Next, we extract the cluster medoids (the centrally representative points of each cluster) utilizing the `extract_medoids` method. By setting the target k to NULL, the algorithm automatically calibrates and selects the optimal number of clusters by maximizing the global silhouette score.

Note that this method does not return an isolated data point. The engine utilizes the `temporal_window_hours` parameter defined in the YAML configuration. For each identified medoid, it returns the physical window surrounding the anomaly timestamp. Now, keep in mind that for this naive yaml configuration, features fed to the Isolation Forest are static ones: they have not been engineered to reflect change over time. Therefore, **the presented time windows are not explanatory of the anomalies**, only at best informative in terms of when they occur.

```{r}
#| label: naive-medoids-extraction
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Medoids Extraction Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)

# Target the threshold where Hartigan's D peaks
th_maxD_naive <- stability_curve_naive$Threshold[which.max(stability_curve_naive$Hartigans_D)]

# The optimal k will be automatically chosen
target_k <- NULL

# Extract anomalies, compute distances, calibrate the tree, and extract medoids in one step
engine <- extract_medoids(engine, threshold = th_maxD_naive, k = target_k)
```

<span id="medoids-ggplot-target" class="flash-target" style="color: #0072B2;">Medoids Plotting Wrapper</span>
```{r}
#| label: medoids-ggplot-function
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Medoid Plot Code"

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)

# Define the medoid plotting wrapper
plot_medoid_trajectories <- function(medoid_engine, plot_title, plot_subtitle, label_style = "numeric", vars_to_plot = NULL) {
  
  raw_medoids <- get_medoids(medoid_engine)
  schema <- get_features(medoid_engine)
  
  # Compute cluster sizes directly from the engine's hierarchical tree
  k_clusters <- length(medoid_engine@medoids)
  cluster_counts <- table(stats::cutree(medoid_engine@hierarchical_tree, k = k_clusters))
  
  # Allow targeting specific variables to prevent visual clutter
  if (is.null(vars_to_plot)) {
    plot_vars <- intersect(
      c(schema$context_variables, schema$target_variables), 
      colnames(raw_medoids)
    )
  } else {
    plot_vars <- intersect(vars_to_plot, colnames(raw_medoids))
  }
  
  format_var_name <- function(x) {
    str_to_title(str_replace_all(str_replace_all(x, "_15m", ""), "_", " "))
  }
  
  # Compute robust global bounds to anchor y-axes
  global_bounds <- medoid_engine@raw_time_course |>
    select(all_of(plot_vars)) |>
    pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
    group_by(Variable) |>
    summarise(
      Min = quantile(Value, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE),
      Max = quantile(Value, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      Variable_Clean = factor(Variable, levels = plot_vars, labels = sapply(plot_vars, format_var_name))
    )
  
  blank_data <- bind_rows(
    global_bounds |> select(Variable_Clean, Value = Min),
    global_bounds |> select(Variable_Clean, Value = Max)
  )
  
  # Prepare plotting data with cluster member counts (n) and Proximity decay
  plot_data <- raw_medoids |>
    mutate(
      Relative_Time = as.numeric(difftime(timestamp, medoid_timestamp, units = "hours")),
      cluster_id = as.numeric(str_extract(cluster, "\\d+")),
      n_members = as.integer(cluster_counts[as.character(cluster_id)]),
      Archetype_Base = if (label_style == "alpha") {
        paste("Archetype", LETTERS[cluster_id])
      } else {
        str_replace(cluster, "Cluster", "Archetype")
      },
      Archetype = sprintf("%s (%d)", Archetype_Base, n_members),
      Proximity = 1 - (abs(Relative_Time) / max(abs(Relative_Time), na.rm = TRUE))
    ) |>
    mutate(
      Archetype = factor(Archetype, levels = unique(Archetype[order(cluster_id)]))
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = all_of(plot_vars),
      names_to = "Variable",
      values_to = "Value"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      Variable_Clean = factor(Variable, levels = plot_vars, labels = sapply(plot_vars, format_var_name))
    )
  
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Relative_Time, y = Value, color = Variable_Clean)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_line(aes(alpha = Proximity, linewidth = Proximity)) +
    geom_point(
      data = function(x) filter(x, Relative_Time == 0), 
      shape = 21, 
      color = "black",          
      size = 3.5,               
      stroke = 0.8,             
      aes(fill = Variable_Clean)
    ) +
    geom_blank(data = blank_data, aes(x = 0, y = Value), inherit.aes = FALSE) + 
    facet_grid(Variable_Clean ~ Archetype, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo") + 
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "turbo") + 
    scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.2, 1), guide = "none") +
    scale_linewidth_continuous(range = c(0.4, 2), guide = "none") +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Relative Time from Anomaly (Hours)",
      y = "Telemetry Value"
    ) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      strip.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, angle = 270), 
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.5),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.spacing = unit(0, "pt"),
      panel.border = element_rect(color = "grey80", fill = NA, linewidth = 1.0)
    )
  
  return(p)
}
```


```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-medoids
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Call Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "Multivariate time-course trajectories for the two extracted HVAC fault archetypes at the maximum Hartigan's D. The physical window spans from two hours before to two hours after the detected anomaly timestamp (dashed vertical line)." 

# Visualization
fig_medoids_naive <- plot_medoid_trajectories(
  engine,
  plot_title = sprintf("Multivariate Trajectories of HVAC Faults (Naive Configuration, T=%.4f)", th_maxD_naive),
  plot_subtitle = "Archetypes extracted at the maximum Hartigan's D threshold."
)

print(fig_medoids_naive)
```


@fig-naive-medoids shows that targeting the maximum distance heterogeneity with $D$ isolated two distinct physical faults. To properly interpret these faults under the naive configuration, we must look only at the anchor points at $t=0$, as these represent the only data the clustering algorithm evaluated.

- **Archetype 1** is characterized at $t=0$ by an actively running system in a warm, humid external environment (high T Outdoor and Rh Outdoor). The system is consuming Power and Energy, and the internal variables reflect an active cooling state with relatively moderate supply and return temperatures. The system might not be able to sufficiently cool the building at this anomaly timestamp.
- **Archetype 2** represents a different state. At $t=0$, the active Power reading sits exactly at zero in a cool, dry external environment. Despite these cooler ambient conditions, the internal temperatures (T Supply, T Return, T Saturation) are anomalously hot—significantly higher than those in Archetype 1. 


In conclusion, targeting the peak of Hartigan's $D$ maximized the distance between an actively powered, internally cool system operating in a warm environment, and an unpowered, internally hot system sitting in a cool environment.

## 4 Engineering Features for the Turin HVAC dataset

Raw sensor channels are static: each observation records the state of the system at a single `timestamp` without capturing how variables evolve over time. To design features that reflect the dynamics of the HVAC unit, we first inspect a continuous one-week window of the raw telemetry.

```{r}
#| label: fig-data-exploration-all
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| dev: "jpeg"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-cap: "1-Week Time Course of All System Variables"

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(isoRouting)

# 1. Load the bundled package data
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")

# 2. Instantiate the engine and ingest data strictly through the API
engine_exploratory <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_naive)
engine_exploratory <- ingest_time_course(engine_exploratory, data = hvac_features)

# 3. Retrieve the validated telemetry using the S4 getter
hvac_valid <- get_time_course(engine_exploratory)

# 4. Extract a 1-week subset for visualization
hvac_week <- hvac_valid |>
  filter(
    timestamp >= ymd("2019-11-01", tz = "UTC"), 
    timestamp < ymd("2019-11-08", tz = "UTC")
  ) 

# 5. Pivot and plot
hvac_plot_all <- hvac_week |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -timestamp, 
    names_to = "Variable", 
    values_to = "Value"
  )

ggplot(hvac_plot_all, aes(x = timestamp, y = Value, color = Variable)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Comprehensive 1-Week HVAC Telemetry",
    subtitle = "Turin Dataset: Nov 1 - Nov 7, 2019",
    x = "Time", 
    y = "Measurement"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

The most prominent characteristics in @fig-data-exploration-all are the step changes across variables like `energy`, `power`, and `t_supply`. These jumps reflect the causal, closed-loop control mechanics of the HVAC system: crossing a programmed threshold triggers a quick mechanical response.

These rapid state transitions also explain the separated clusters and sharp boundaries seen earlier in @fig-pairs-plot. Because the unit switches quickly between discrete operating regimes, pairwise scatterplots appear as isolated lines and dense clouds with few intermediate values. To capture the transitions that govern the unit's physical behavior, we must engineer temporal features—such as short-term differences and state durations—that encode rates of change [@blazquez2021review; @cook2019anomaly].

The following subsections examine the raw variable distributions and state transitions to design each engineered feature.

### 4.1 Power and Energy

```{r}
#| label: fig-energy-power-mechanics
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Code"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Top: Distributions of Energy and Power. Bottom: Transition matrices detailing the frequency of state changes (static continuous states are filtered out to highlight active transitions)."

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(patchwork)

# Define uniform factor levels to ensure heatmaps align correctly
state_levels <- c("Low", "Medium", "High")

# --- 1. Top Row: Histograms ---
p_hist_energy <- hvac_valid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = energy)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 150, fill = "#3b528b", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Energy Distribution", x = "Energy", y = "Count") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

p_hist_power <- hvac_valid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = power)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 150, fill = "#21918c", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Power Distribution", x = "Power", y = "Count") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

# --- 2. Data Prep: Transition Matrices ---
# Energy transitions
trans_energy <- hvac_valid |>
  select(timestamp, energy) |>
  mutate(
    state = case_when(
      energy >= 0 & energy < 5 ~ "Low",
      energy >= 5 & energy < 10 ~ "Medium",
      energy >= 10 ~ "High"
    ),
    state = factor(state, levels = state_levels),
    prev_state = lag(state)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(prev_state) & state != prev_state) |>
  count(prev_state, state, name = "Count")

# Power transitions
trans_power <- hvac_valid |>
  select(timestamp, power) |>
  mutate(
    state = case_when(
      power >= 0 & power < 2 ~ "Low",
      power >= 2 & power < 4 ~ "Medium",
      power >= 4 ~ "High"
    ),
    state = factor(state, levels = state_levels),
    prev_state = lag(state)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(prev_state) & state != prev_state) |>
  count(prev_state, state, name = "Count")

# --- 3. Bottom Row: Heatmaps ---
plot_heatmap <- function(data, title, fill_color) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = prev_state, y = state, fill = Count)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = Count), color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey80", high = fill_color) +
    scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    scale_y_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Previous State", y = "New State") +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
}

p_heat_energy <- plot_heatmap(trans_energy, "Energy Transitions", "#3b528b")
p_heat_power <- plot_heatmap(trans_power, "Power Transitions", "#21918c")

# --- 4. Combine with Patchwork ---
layout <- (p_hist_energy | p_hist_power) / (p_heat_energy | p_heat_power)
layout + plot_annotation(
  title = "Power and Energy: Distributions and Transitions",
  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"))
)
```

@fig-energy-power-mechanics displays the distributions and state transitions for energy and power. The top histograms show that both variables operate in three discrete bands: Low (off/standby), Medium (partial load), and High (full load). The transition heatmaps in the bottom row show that the control loop frequently bypasses the intermediate state, relying heavily on direct Low-to-High and High-to-Low jumps. Because a simple first difference ($\Delta_{15m} = x_t - x_{t-1}$) treats a Low-to-Medium step ($\approx 0 \to 3$) and a Medium-to-High step ($\approx 3 \to 5.5$) as having similar magnitudes, we capture transitions with 15-minute differences weighted by the current load level:

$$\text{dw\_x}(t) = x(t) \cdot \bigl(x(t) - x(t - 1)\bigr)$$
This weighted derivative amplifies transitions that terminate at high power or energy loads and suppresses minor fluctuations near standby.

```{r}
#| label: prep-energy-power-mismatch
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Energy and Power State Co-occurrence"

library(dplyr)

state_levels <- c("Low", "Medium", "High")

# Prepare co-occurrence data
mismatch_data <- hvac_valid |>
  select(timestamp, energy, power) |>
  mutate(
    energy_state = factor(case_when(
      energy >= 0 & energy < 5  ~ "Low",
      energy >= 5 & energy < 10 ~ "Medium",
      energy >= 10              ~ "High"
    ), levels = state_levels),
    power_state = factor(case_when(
      power >= 0 & power < 2 ~ "Low",
      power >= 2 & power < 4 ~ "Medium",
      power >= 4             ~ "High"
    ), levels = state_levels)
  ) |>
  count(energy_state, power_state, name = "Count")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-energy-power-mismatch
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Co-occurrence matrix of Energy and Power states. Off-diagonal tiles represent temporal desynchronization where instantaneous power and accumulated energy do not perfectly align."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mismatch_data, aes(x = energy_state, y = power_state, fill = Count)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  # Dynamically change text color based on background darkness
  geom_text(aes(label = Count, color = Count > 1000), fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "white")) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "#e34a33", trans = "log10") +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  scale_y_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Energy vs. Power: State Co-occurrence",
    x     = "Energy State (15-min Accumulated)",
    y     = "Power State (Instantaneous)"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid      = element_blank(),
    axis.text       = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
Although energy and power are strongly coupled across the time course, @fig-energy-power-mismatch reveals off-diagonal state mismatches where instantaneous power and 15-minute accumulated energy temporarily diverge during switching intervals. To preserve these desynchronizations as potential fault indicators, we include both weighted derivatives in the engineered feature set:

`dw_power(t) = power(t)(power(t)-power(t-1))`<br>
`dw_energy(t) = energy(t)(energy(t)-energy(t-1))`

#### Run-Length Features

We now examine the distributions of times spent in each `energy` and `power` mode (Low, Medium an High). We call these times *dwell times*. 


```{r}
#| label: prep-energy-power-mode-rle
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Energy and Power Mode RLE Durations"

library(dplyr)

# 1. Classify Energy and Power into their discrete operating modes
ep_modes <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  select(timestamp, energy, power) |>
  filter(!is.na(energy) & !is.na(power)) |>
  mutate(
    energy_mode = case_when(
      energy < 2.5  ~ "Low",
      energy <= 7.5 ~ "Medium",
      TRUE          ~ "High"
    ),
    power_mode = case_when(
      power < 1.0   ~ "Low",
      power <= 4.0  ~ "Medium",
      TRUE          ~ "High"
    )
  )

# 2. Helper to extract RLE durations (in hours) for each mode
extract_mode_runs <- function(mode_vec, var_name) {
  runs <- rle(mode_vec)
  data.frame(
    variable       = var_name,
    mode           = factor(runs$values, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),
    length_15m     = runs$lengths,
    duration_hours = runs$lengths * 0.25
  )
}

mode_runs_df <- bind_rows(
  extract_mode_runs(ep_modes$energy_mode, "Energy"),
  extract_mode_runs(ep_modes$power_mode,  "Power")
)

# 3. Summary stats (Median, 95th percentile, and Max hours) for panel annotations
mode_stats <- mode_runs_df |>
  group_by(variable, mode) |>
  summarise(
    n_runs  = n(),
    med_hrs = median(duration_hours),
    q95_hrs = quantile(duration_hours, 0.95),
    max_hrs = max(duration_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    label = sprintf(
      "Runs: %d\nMed: %.2f h\n95%%: %.1f h\nMax: %.1f h",
      n_runs, med_hrs, q95_hrs, max_hrs
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-energy-power-mode-rle
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of continuous dwell times (in hours) spent in Low, Medium, and High operating modes for Energy and Power."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mode_runs_df, aes(x = duration_hours, fill = mode)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, boundary = 0, color = "black", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ mode, scales = "free") +
  geom_text(
    data = mode_stats,
    aes(x = Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.1, fontface = "bold", size = 3.2, color = "grey20"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Low" = "#3b528b", "Medium" = "#21918c", "High" = "#5ec962")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 24)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title    = "Dwell-Time Distributions by Operating Mode (Energy & Power)",
    subtitle = "Continuous hours spent in Low, Medium, and High states (x-axis zoomed to 0-24h)",
    x        = "Continuous Dwell Time (Hours)",
    y        = "Number of Runs"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

@fig-energy-power-mode-rle reveals wide distributions. Notice some peaks likely driven by programmed building schedules—such as the $9.5$-hour overnight shutdown peak in Low and the $9$- to $16$-hour daytime operating peaks in High. 

Still, because these distributions remain wide, we next examine how adding these 6 dwell-time variables to the Isolation Forest training changes the distribution of anomaly scores, as compared to the final set of 24 engineered features we will ultimately select.

```{r}
#| label: prep-score-compression-24-vs-30
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: 24 vs. 30 Features Anomaly Scoring"

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(isotree)

# 1. Generate the 6 mode dwell-time columns in memory on hvac_features
get_mode_rl <- function(val_vec, low_cut, high_cut, target_mode) {
  mode_chr <- case_when(
    is.na(val_vec)      ~ "Missing",
    val_vec < low_cut   ~ "Low",
    val_vec <= high_cut ~ "Medium",
    TRUE                ~ "High"
  )
  tibble(m = mode_chr, grp = consecutive_id(mode_chr)) |>
    group_by(grp) |>
    mutate(rl = if_else(m == target_mode, as.numeric(row_number()), 0)) |>
    pull(rl)
}

df_comp <- hvac_features |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  mutate(
    power_low_run_len   = get_mode_rl(power,  1.0, 4.0, "Low"),
    power_med_run_len   = get_mode_rl(power,  1.0, 4.0, "Medium"),
    power_high_run_len  = get_mode_rl(power,  1.0, 4.0, "High"),
    energy_low_run_len  = get_mode_rl(energy, 2.5, 7.5, "Low"),
    energy_med_run_len  = get_mode_rl(energy, 2.5, 7.5, "Medium"),
    energy_high_run_len = get_mode_rl(energy, 2.5, 7.5, "High")
  )

vars_24 <- c(
  "dw_power", "dw_energy", "d_rh_outdoor", "d_t_outdoor",
  "d_t_return_15m", "t_ret_run_length", "t_ret_displacement",
  "control_error", "supply_delta",
  "d_t_supply_15m", "t_sup_run_length", "t_sup_displacement",
  "humidity_delta", "supply_margin", "return_margin",
  "d_humidity_delta_15m", "run_length_humidity_delta", "displacement_humidity_delta",
  "d_supply_margin_15m", "run_length_supply_margin", "displacement_supply_margin",
  "d_return_margin_15m", "run_length_return_margin", "displacement_return_margin"
)

vars_30 <- c(
  vars_24,
  "power_low_run_len", "power_med_run_len", "power_high_run_len",
  "energy_low_run_len", "energy_med_run_len", "energy_high_run_len"
)

fit_and_score <- function(df, cols) {
  set.seed(42)
  mat <- as.matrix(df[, cols])
  iso <- isolation.forest(mat, ntrees = 500, sample_size = 256, seed = 42, missing_action = "fail")
  predict(iso, mat)
}

scores_24_30 <- tibble(
  `24 Features (Core Engineered)` = fit_and_score(df_comp, vars_24),
  `30 Features (+6 Mode Dwell)`   = fit_and_score(df_comp, vars_30)
) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Configuration", values_to = "Score") |>
  mutate(Configuration = factor(
    Configuration,
    levels = c("24 Features (Core Engineered)", "30 Features (+6 Mode Dwell)")
  ))

# 2. Compute tail summary statistics for plot annotations (cutoff = 0.50)
tail_stats <- scores_24_30 |>
  group_by(Configuration) |>
  summarise(
    n_50    = sum(Score >= 0.50),
    n_60    = sum(Score >= 0.60),
    max_s   = max(Score),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    label = sprintf(
      "Count (Score >= 0.50): %d\nCount (Score >= 0.60): %d\nMax Score: %.3f",
      n_50, n_60, max_s
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-score-compression-24-vs-30
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of Isolation Forest anomaly score distributions for the 24-feature core configuration versus the 30-feature configuration (+6 mode dwell-time counters). Top: Full score density overlay showing probability mass shifting from the right tail (>= 0.50) into the 0.35-0.42 bulk. Bottom: Upper-tail histograms (Score >= 0.50) on an identical y-axis."

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# High-contrast Okabe-Ito palette: Vermilion Orange-Red vs. Navy Blue
palette_contrast <- c(
  "24 Features (Core Engineered)" = "#D55E00",
  "30 Features (+6 Mode Dwell)"   = "#0072B2"
)

# 1. Top Panel: Full Anomaly Score Density Overlay
p_density <- ggplot(scores_24_30, aes(x = Score, fill = Configuration, color = Configuration)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.28, linewidth = 1.0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.50, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 0.505, y = 14, label = "Tail Cutoff (0.50) ->",
    hjust = 0, fontface = "italic", size = 3.5, color = "grey20"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette_contrast) +
  scale_color_manual(values = palette_contrast) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title    = "A. Full Anomaly Score Density Distributions (24 vs. 30 Features)",
    subtitle = "Adding 6 mode dwell-time counters shifts probability mass from the right tail (>= 0.50) into the 0.35-0.42 bulk",
    x        = "Anomaly Score",
    y        = "Density"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

# 2. Bottom Panel: Upper Tail Comparison (Score >= 0.50) with Fixed Y-Axis
p_tail <- ggplot(filter(scores_24_30, Score >= 0.50), aes(x = Score, fill = Configuration, color = Configuration)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.005, boundary = 0.50, alpha = 0.65, color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~Configuration, ncol = 1, scales = "fixed") +
  geom_text(
    data = tail_stats,
    aes(x = Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1.08, vjust = 1.25, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, color = "grey15"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette_contrast) +
  scale_color_manual(values = palette_contrast) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title    = "B. Upper Tail Comparison (Anomaly Score >= 0.50)",
    subtitle = "Adding 6 mode dwell-time counters reduces observations with Score >= 0.60 from 194 to 15",
    x        = "Anomaly Score",
    y        = "Observation Count"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

# 3. Combine with patchwork
p_density / p_tail + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.35))
```

@fig-score-compression-24-vs-30 shows a drop in high anomaly scores when the 6 dwell-time counters are added to the final set of 24 features. This suggests that the added counters are not beneficial to anomaly detection, but instead detrimental.

Now, the decrease in the anomaly score tail could be due to the dimension jump from 24 to 30 features. To confirm that the tail reduction is indeed caused by incorporating the dwell-time counters, we perform a fixed-dimension control experiment: the Isolation Forest is always trained on exactly 24 features drawn without replacement from the 30-feature pool using identical hyperparameters (`ntrees = 500`, `sample_size = 256`, `seed = 42`). We first evaluate 200 unconditional random subsets to establish an unbiased null distribution. Because subsets containing only one or two dwell-time counters rarely occur under uniform random draws, we supplement the experiment with 15 targeted random subsets for each of those two strata so the full dilution trajectory is visible across all counter counts ($k = 1$ through $6$). The results are summarized in @fig-mc-feature-subset-control.

```{r}
#| label: prep-mc-feature-subset-control
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Exact Monte Carlo 24-of-30 Feature Subset Permutation Test"

library(dplyr)
library(isotree)
library(parallel)

# 1. Prepare the 30-feature matrix (24 core + 6 mode dwell counters)
dwell_cols <- c(
  "power_low_run_len", "power_med_run_len", "power_high_run_len",
  "energy_low_run_len", "energy_med_run_len", "energy_high_run_len"
)

mat_30  <- as.matrix(df_comp[, vars_30])

chk <- Sys.getenv("_R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_", "")
n_cores <- if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") {
  1L
} else if (nzchar(chk) && chk != "FALSE") {
  2L
} else {
  min(4L, max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 1L))
}
# 2. Evaluate the actual 24-feature core configuration (ntrees = 100, seed = 42)
ntrees_mc <- 100L
iso_core <- isolation.forest(
  mat_30[, vars_24], ntrees = ntrees_mc, sample_size = 256,
  nthreads = 1L, seed = 42, missing_action = "fail"
)
scores_core      <- predict(iso_core, mat_30[, vars_24], nthreads = 1L)
obs_tail_mass_50 <- mean(scores_core >= 0.50)

# 3. Generate M = 100 unconditional random 24-feature subsets (for Panel A & p-value)
M <- 100L
set.seed(2026)
uncond_subsets <- lapply(seq_len(M), function(i) {
  sample(vars_30, size = 24, replace = FALSE)
})

# Supplement rare hypergeometric strata (k = 1 and k = 2) with 15 random subsets each
# so Panel B displays the full stepwise dilution curve across all k in {1..6}
sample_fixed_k <- function(k_target, n_reps) {
  lapply(seq_len(n_reps), function(i) {
    c(
      sample(dwell_cols, size = k_target, replace = FALSE),
      sample(vars_24, size = 24L - k_target, replace = FALSE)
    )
  })
}

supp_subsets <- c(sample_fixed_k(1L, 15L), sample_fixed_k(2L, 15L))
all_subsets  <- c(uncond_subsets, supp_subsets)
is_uncond    <- c(rep(TRUE, M), rep(FALSE, length(supp_subsets)))

# 4. Evaluate each fixed 24-feature subset using an exact 500-tree Isolation Forest
mc_workers <- if (.Platform$OS.type == "unix") n_cores else 1L

mc_all <- parallel::mclapply(seq_along(all_subsets), function(i) {
  sampled_vars <- all_subsets[[i]]
  n_dwell_in   <- sum(sampled_vars %in% dwell_cols)
  sub_mat      <- mat_30[, sampled_vars]
  
  iso_m <- isolation.forest(
    sub_mat, ntrees = ntrees_mc, sample_size = 256,
    nthreads = 1L, seed = 42, missing_action = "fail"
  )
  sc_m <- predict(iso_m, sub_mat, nthreads = 1L)
  
  tibble(
    iter          = i,
    unconditional = is_uncond[i],
    n_dwell       = factor(n_dwell_in, levels = as.character(0:6)),
    tail_mass_50  = mean(sc_m >= 0.50)
  )
}, mc.cores = mc_workers) |> bind_rows()

# Separate unconditional null draws (Panel A) from full stratified draws (Panel B)
mc_uncond <- filter(mc_all, unconditional)

# 5. Compute exact Phipson-Smyth permutation p-value on the unconditional draws
emp_pct <- 100 * mean(mc_uncond$tail_mass_50 <= obs_tail_mass_50)
p_val   <- (1 + sum(mc_uncond$tail_mass_50 >= obs_tail_mass_50)) / (M + 1)

# 6. Reference point for the core 24-feature configuration (0 dwell counters)
core_point_df <- tibble(
  n_dwell      = factor("0", levels = as.character(0:6)),
  tail_mass_50 = obs_tail_mass_50
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mc-feature-subset-control
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Monte Carlo permutation distribution of upper-tail probability mass P(Score >= 0.50) across random subsets of 24 features drawn without replacement from the 30-feature pool (ntrees = 100). Left: Unconditional null distribution of 100 random 24-feature subsets versus the actual 24-feature core configuration (dashed orange-red line). Right: Stepwise dilution of upper-tail mass across all mode dwell-time counter counts k in {0, ..., 6}, with k = 1, 2 supplemented by 15 stratified draws each."

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# 1. Panel A: Histogram of unconditional random 24-feature subsets
p_hist_mc <- ggplot(mc_uncond, aes(x = tail_mass_50 * 100)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#0072B2", color = "white", alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_tail_mass_50 * 100, color = "#D55E00", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = obs_tail_mass_50 * 100, y = Inf,
    label = sprintf("Core 24 Set\n(%.2f%%, p = %.4f)", obs_tail_mass_50 * 100, p_val),
    hjust = 1.08, vjust = 1.4, fontface = "bold", color = "#D55E00", size = 3.5
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  labs(
    title    = "A. Null Distribution of Tail Mass (d = 24)",
    subtitle = sprintf("%d random 24-of-30 subsets (ntrees = %d)", M, ntrees_mc),
    x        = "Upper-Tail Mass (% Score >= 0.50)",
    y        = "Number of Random Subsets"
  )

# 2. Panel B: Stepwise Dilution by Number of Included Mode Dwell Counters (0 to 6)
p_dwell_effect <- ggplot(mc_all, aes(x = n_dwell, y = tail_mass_50 * 100)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.35, outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(aes(shape = unconditional), width = 0.15, alpha = 0.7, color = "#2C7BB6") +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 2),
    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Unconditional (Panel A)", `FALSE` = "Stratified (k = 1, 2)"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = core_point_df,
    aes(x = n_dwell, y = tail_mass_50 * 100),
    color = "#D55E00", size = 4.5, shape = 18
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = "0", y = obs_tail_mass_50 * 100,
    label = "Core 24",
    hjust = -0.25, vjust = 0.5, fontface = "bold", color = "#D55E00", size = 3.4
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(
    title    = "B. Impact of Mode Dwell Counters",
    subtitle = "Tail mass vs. dwell counter count at fixed d = 24",
    x        = "Mode Dwell Counters Included (d = 24)",
    y        = "Upper-Tail Mass (% Score >= 0.50)"
  )

(p_hist_mc | p_dwell_effect) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

As shown in Panel A, every unconditional random 24-feature combination places only $1.1\%$ to $4.0\%$ of observations in the high-score tail ($\text{Score} \ge 0.50$), whereas our core 24-feature set—the only combination with zero dwell-time counters—reaches $4.97\%$ ($p = 0.0050$). Panel B demonstrates a continuous, monotonic contraction across the entire range: the more dwell-time counters a 24-feature subset includes, the further the high-score tail shrinks, dropping from a median of $4.3\%$ when a single counter is included down to $1.8\%$ when all six are present.

In conclusion, due to the fact that they tend to reduce anomaly scores, dwell-time counters are not included as engineered features. Only weighted derivatives are included for `power` and `energy`.
          

### 4.2 Outdoor Environmental Variables

Unlike the abrupt mechanical step-changes of the HVAC equipment, outdoor environmental variables (`rh_outdoor` and `t_outdoor`) vary slowly and continuously over time. We confirm this smoothness across the dataset by checking two standard metrics: the lag-1 autocorrelation (which remains close to 1 for smooth series) and the ratio of standard deviations of step changes and raw values (which remains small for smooth series).

```{r}
#| label: smoothness-quantification
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true

library(dplyr)
library(stats)

hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  summarise(
    rh_autocorrelation = acf(rh_outdoor, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE, na.action = na.pass)$acf[2],
    rh_sd_ratio = sd(rh_outdoor - lag(rh_outdoor), na.rm = TRUE) / sd(rh_outdoor, na.rm = TRUE),
    t_autocorrelation = acf(t_outdoor, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE, na.action = na.pass)$acf[2],
    t_sd_ratio = sd(t_outdoor - lag(t_outdoor), na.rm = TRUE) / sd(t_outdoor, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  print()
```

The results confirm the continuous nature of these environmental features: both variables yield high autocorrelations (>0.99) and low step-to-raw variation ratios (<0.14).

```{r}
#| label: prep-outdoor-environment
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Outdoor Weather"

library(dplyr)

# Calculate 15-minute step changes
outdoor_features <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  select(timestamp, rh_outdoor, t_outdoor) |>
  mutate(
    rh_15m_diff = rh_outdoor - lag(rh_outdoor, n = 1),
    t_15m_diff  = t_outdoor - lag(t_outdoor, n = 1)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-outdoor-environment
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of raw values and 15-minute changes for outdoor relative humidity (left) and temperature (right). The narrow distributions of the changes highlight the slow, continuous nature of environmental shifts."

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# --- 1. RH Plots (Left Column) ---
p_rh_raw <- ggplot(outdoor_features, aes(x = rh_outdoor)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#440154", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Outdoor Humidity (Raw)", x = "Relative Humidity (%)", y = "Count")

p_rh_diff <- ggplot(outdoor_features, aes(x = rh_15m_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#440154", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "15-Minute Step Change", x = "\u0394 RH (%)", y = "Count")

# --- 2. Temp Plots (Right Column) ---
p_t_raw <- ggplot(outdoor_features, aes(x = t_outdoor)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#c22b38", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Outdoor Temperature (Raw)", x = "Temperature (\u00B0C)", y = "Count")

p_t_diff <- ggplot(outdoor_features, aes(x = t_15m_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#c22b38", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "15-Minute Step Change", x = "\u0394 Temperature (\u00B0C)", y = "Count")

# --- 3. Combine with Patchwork ---
(p_rh_raw | p_t_raw) / (p_rh_diff | p_t_diff) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Outdoor Weather Sensors",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"))
  )
```

As shown in the bottom panels of @fig-outdoor-environment, the 15-minute changes for both temperature and humidity are tightly clustered around zero. This narrow baseline makes the 15-minute step change an effective feature for anomaly detection, allowing the Isolation Forest to easily spot unusual weather events (such as sudden temperature drops during storms) or sensor errors (such as abrupt humidity dropouts).

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{d\_rh\_outdoor}(t) &= \text{rh\_outdoor}(t) - \text{rh\_outdoor}(t-1) \\
\text{d\_t\_outdoor}(t) &= \text{t\_outdoor}(t) - \text{t\_outdoor}(t-1)
\end{aligned}$$


### 4.3 Indoor Return Temperature (`t_return`)

To explore the behavior of `t_return`, we first examine its raw distribution alongside its 15-minute and 1-hour temporal derivatives.

```{r}
#| label: prep-t-return-histograms
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Return Temperature Derivatives"

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

t_return_eda <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  select(timestamp, t_return) |>
  mutate(
    t_ret_15m_diff = t_return - lag(t_return, n = 1),
    t_ret_1h_diff  = t_return - lag(t_return, n = 4)
  )

t_ret_long <- t_return_eda |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(t_return, t_ret_15m_diff, t_ret_1h_diff),
    names_to  = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(
      metric,
      levels = c("t_return", "t_ret_15m_diff", "t_ret_1h_diff"),
      labels = c("Raw t_return (\u00B0C)", "15-Minute Derivative (\u0394 15m)", "1-Hour Derivative (\u0394 1h)")
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t-return-histograms
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of raw values and temporal derivatives for return temperature across the full dataset."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(t_ret_long, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#c22b38", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

Unlike outdoor environmental variables, the distribution of `t_return` is smooth and continuous, lacking coarse sensor discretization. In addition, the extended tails of the 1-hour derivative compared to the tight 15-minute derivative suggest that temperature changes compound over time. This hints at the presence of prolonged, continuous periods of active heating or cooling. To quantify the durations of these continuous phases, we apply Run Length Encoding (RLE). We classify 15-minute intervals with a derivative $> 0.05^\circ\text{C}$ as *heating* and $< -0.05^\circ\text{C}$ as *cooling*, and calculate the total consecutive time spent in each state.

```{r}
#| label: prep-t-return-run-histograms
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Return Temperature RLE Durations"

library(dplyr)

t_return_runs <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  mutate(
    t_ret_15m_diff = t_return - lag(t_return),
    diff_sign = case_when(
      t_ret_15m_diff > 0.05  ~ "Heating (Increasing)",
      t_ret_15m_diff < -0.05 ~ "Cooling (Decreasing)",
      TRUE                   ~ "Stable"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(diff_sign))

runs <- rle(t_return_runs$diff_sign)

run_df <- data.frame(
  state                = runs$values, length_15m_intervals = runs$lengths
) |>
  filter(state != "Stable") |>
  mutate(duration_hours = length_15m_intervals * 0.25)

anno_df <- run_df |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(
    max_hrs = max(duration_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("Max Duration:\n", max_hrs, " hours"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t-return-run-histograms
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Histogram of continuous heating and cooling durations, calculated using Run Length Encoding on the sign of the 15-minute derivative."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(run_df, aes(x = duration_hours, fill = state)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, color = "black", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~state, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  geom_text(
    data = anno_df,
    aes(x = 4.8, y = c(1000, 1000), label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4, color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Cooling (Decreasing)" = "#3b528b", "Heating (Increasing)" = "#c22b38")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 5, by = 0.5)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 5)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(x = "Continuous Duration (Hours)", y = "Count of Occurrences") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

@fig-t-return-run-histograms shows that continuous operational states can persist for nearly 6 hours.

To help the Isolation Forest recognize anomalous prolonged cooling and heating events, we incorporate two engineered features:

* **Signed Duration (`t_ret_run_length`)**: An integer counter of how many consecutive intervals the system has been moving in the current direction (positive for heating, negative for cooling). This represents time spent in a continuous state.
* **Cumulative Displacement (`t_ret_displacement`)**: The total temperature change since the current continuous run began. This captures the intensity of the state, separating passive environmental drift (long duration, low displacement) from active mechanical forcing (long duration, high displacement).

These features are defined as:

$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta \text{t\_return}_{15m}(t) &= \text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_return}(t-1) \\
\text{t\_ret\_run\_length}(t) &= k \times \text{direction} \\
\text{t\_ret\_displacement}(t) &= \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \Delta \text{t\_return}_{15m}(t-i)
\end{aligned}$$

where $k$ represents the number of consecutive 15-minute intervals in the current thermal `direction` (-1 for cooling and +1 for heating).


### 4.4 System Error, Thermal Effort, and Thermal Kinematics (`sp_return` & `t_supply`)

The variables `sp_return` (programmed setpoint) and `t_supply` (air exiting the mechanical unit) are final key controls of the HVAC loop. Their independent values do not directly convey the system's performance. For instance, a raw `t_supply` of $22^\circ\text{C}$ represents active heating if the room is $18^\circ\text{C}$, but represents active cooling if the room is $26^\circ\text{C}$.

To provide the Isolation Forest with a better geometric manifold of the system's physical state, we engineer these relationships into two temperature gaps:

```{r}
#| label: prep-system-gaps
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Control Error and Supply Delta"

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

gaps_eda <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  select(timestamp, t_return, sp_return, t_supply) |>
  mutate(
    control_error = t_return - sp_return,
    supply_delta  = t_supply - t_return
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(control_error) & !is.na(supply_delta))

gaps_long <- gaps_eda |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(control_error, supply_delta),
    names_to  = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(
      metric,
      levels = c("control_error", "supply_delta"),
      labels = c(
        "Control Error (t_return - sp_return)",
        "Supply Delta (t_supply - t_return)"
      )
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-system-gaps
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of the Control Error (top) and Supply Delta (bottom). The Supply Delta captures the operational states: idling (the central spike at zero), active cooling (the left tail), active heating (the right mound), and extreme mechanical anomalies (the distant outliers)."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(gaps_long, aes(x = value, fill = metric)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 150, color = "black", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#3b528b", "#e35932")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(x = "Temperature Difference (\u00B0C)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

* **Control Error (`control_error`)**: The difference between the actual room state and the programmed target: 't_return' - 'sp_return'. As shown in @fig-system-gaps (top), this yields a broad, negatively skewed distribution. Large deviations in this feature allow the algorithm to isolate moments where the system is failing to keep up with the environmental load.
* **Thermal Effort (`supply_delta`)**: The temperature difference ($\Delta T$) across the room: `t_supply - t_return`. As shown in @fig-system-gaps (bottom), this cleanly separates the system's operational phases, isolating extreme mechanical effort (distant outliers) from standard idling or active cycles.

Next, as we did with `t_return`, we explore the durations of active heating and cooling periods as defined by `t_supply`.

```{r}
#| label: prep-t-supply-run-histograms
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Supply Temperature RLE Durations"

library(dplyr)

supply_runs <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  mutate(
    t_sup_15m_diff = t_supply - lag(t_supply),
    diff_sign = case_when(
      t_sup_15m_diff > 0.05  ~ "Heating (Increasing)",
```
