```{r}
      t_sup_15m_diff < -0.05 ~ "Cooling (Decreasing)",
      TRUE                   ~ "Stable"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(diff_sign))

runs <- rle(supply_runs$diff_sign)

run_df <- data.frame(
  state                = runs$values, length_15m_intervals = runs$lengths
) |>
  filter(state != "Stable") |>
  mutate(duration_hours = length_15m_intervals * 0.25)

anno_df <- run_df |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(
    max_hrs = max(duration_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("Max Duration:\n", max_hrs, " hours"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t-supply-run-histograms
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Histogram of continuous heating and cooling durations for supply air."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(run_df, aes(x = duration_hours, fill = state)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, color = "black", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~state, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  geom_text(
    data = anno_df,
    aes(x = Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1.2, vjust = 1.5, fontface = "bold", size = 4, color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Cooling (Decreasing)" = "#3b528b", "Heating (Increasing)" = "#e35932")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 0.5)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(x = "Continuous Duration (Hours)", y = "Count of Occurrences") +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

@fig-t-supply-run-histograms shows that modulation phases can persist for up to 6 hours. To equip the Isolation Forest to detect these prolonged periods, we incorporate the following features:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{control\_error}(t) &= \text{t\_return}(t) - \text{sp\_return}(t) \\
\text{supply\_delta}(t) &= \text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_return}(t) \\
\Delta \text{t\_supply}_{15m}(t) &= \text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_supply}(t-1) \\
\text{t\_sup\_run\_length}(t) &= j \times \text{direction} \\
\text{t\_sup\_displacement}(t) &= \sum_{i=0}^{j-1} \Delta \text{t\_supply}_{15m}(t-i)
\end{aligned}$$

where $j$ represents the number of consecutive 15-minute intervals moving in the same thermodynamic direction.


### 4.5 Humidity and Condensation (`rh_return`, `rh_supply` & `t_saturation`)

Variables `rh_return`, `rh_supply`, and `t_saturation` monitor and control the moisture state of the HVAC system. Relative humidity and saturation temperature are inherently coupled to air temperature.

To map these relationships, we engineer three primary differences:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{humidity\_delta}(t) &= \text{rh\_supply}(t) - \text{rh\_return}(t) \\
\text{supply\_margin}(t) &= \text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t) \\
\text{return\_margin}(t) &= \text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t)
\end{aligned}$$

```{r}
#| label: prep-moisture-gaps
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Moisture Gaps and Saturation Margins"

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

moisture_gaps_eda <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  select(timestamp, rh_return, rh_supply, t_supply, t_return, t_saturation) |>
  mutate(
    humidity_delta = rh_supply - rh_return,
    supply_margin  = t_supply - t_saturation,
    return_margin  = t_return - t_saturation
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(humidity_delta) & !is.na(supply_margin) & !is.na(return_margin))

moisture_long <- moisture_gaps_eda |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(humidity_delta, supply_margin, return_margin),
    names_to  = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(
      metric,
      levels = c("humidity_delta", "supply_margin", "return_margin"),
      labels = c(
        "Humidity Delta (rh_supply - rh_return) [%]",
        "Supply Margin (t_supply - t_saturation) [\u00B0C]",
        "Return Margin (t_return - t_saturation) [\u00B0C]"
      )
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-moisture-gaps
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of the engineered moisture gaps: Humidity Delta, Supply Margin, and Return Margin."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(moisture_long, aes(x = value, fill = metric)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 150, color = "black", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#0868ac", "#7bccc4", "#43a2ca")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title    = "Moisture Gaps and Saturation Margins",
    subtitle = "Distributions of engineered humidity and saturation relationships",
    x        = "Difference",
    y        = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

As shown in @fig-moisture-gaps, the Humidity Delta maintains a broadly positive distribution, reflecting an average trend toward active humidification during winter operations. The Supply Margin reveals multiple distinct operational clusters, notably including a probability mass dropping into negative territory. The Return Margin exhibits both negative and positive components, though its distribution is less complex than that of the Supply Margin.

Providing the Isolation Forest with these engineered features allows it to map different moisture regimes to geometric manifolds for anomaly detection.

To determine if these moisture boundaries shift instantaneously or drift over time, we apply the same Run Length Encoding (RLE) methodology previously established for temperature.

```{r}
#| label: prep-moisture-gaps-rle
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Moisture Gaps RLE Durations"

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# 1. Calculate the gaps and their 15m differences
moisture_rle_data <- hvac_valid |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  mutate(
    humidity_delta = rh_supply - rh_return,
    supply_margin  = t_supply - t_saturation,
    return_margin  = t_return - t_saturation
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hum_delta_diff  = humidity_delta - lag(humidity_delta),
    sup_margin_diff = supply_margin - lag(supply_margin),
    ret_margin_diff = return_margin - lag(return_margin)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(hum_delta_diff) & !is.na(sup_margin_diff) & !is.na(ret_margin_diff))

# 2. Helper function to compute RLE for a given vector
compute_rle <- function(diff_vec, threshold, var_name) {
  directions <- case_when(
    diff_vec > threshold  ~ "Increasing",
    diff_vec < -threshold ~ "Decreasing",
    TRUE                  ~ "Stable"
  )
  
  runs <- rle(directions)
  
  data.frame(
    variable   = var_name,
    state      = runs$values, length_15m = runs$lengths
  ) |>
    filter(state != "Stable") |>
    mutate(duration_hours = length_15m * 0.25)
}

# 3. Apply RLE to each gap
rle_hum <- compute_rle(moisture_rle_data$hum_delta_diff,  threshold = 0.1,  "Humidity Delta (%)")
rle_sup <- compute_rle(moisture_rle_data$sup_margin_diff, threshold = 0.05, "Supply Margin (\u00B0C)")
rle_ret <- compute_rle(moisture_rle_data$ret_margin_diff, threshold = 0.05, "Return Margin (\u00B0C)")

# Combine into one dataframe
all_runs <- bind_rows(rle_hum, rle_sup, rle_ret) |>
  mutate(
    variable = factor(
      variable,
      levels = c("Humidity Delta (%)", "Supply Margin (\u00B0C)", "Return Margin (\u00B0C)")
    )
  )

# 4. Compute maximum durations for text annotations
anno_df <- all_runs |>
  group_by(variable, state) |>
  summarise(
    max_hrs = max(duration_hours),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("Max:\n", max_hrs, " h"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-moisture-gaps-rle
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Histograms of consecutive continuous ramping durations for the engineered moisture gaps."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(all_runs, aes(x = duration_hours, fill = state)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, color = "black", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ state, scales = "free_y") +
  geom_text(
    data = anno_df,
    aes(x = Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1.2, vjust = 1.5, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, color = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Decreasing" = "#3b528b", "Increasing" = "#e35932")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 15, by = 1)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title    = "Continuous Ramping Durations for Moisture Gaps",
    subtitle = "Histograms of consecutive increasing/decreasing trajectories",
    x        = "Continuous Duration (Hours)",
    y        = "Count of Occurrences"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

As demonstrated in @fig-moisture-gaps-rle, while the majority of shifts resolve rapidly, the system also undergoes continuous moisture ramps stretching across several hours. Incorporating the temporal history of these margins is essential to fully characterize HVAC performance. This history is encoded via signed duration (run length) and cumulative displacement:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{humidity\_delta}(t) &= \text{rh\_supply}(t) - \text{rh\_return}(t) \\
\text{supply\_margin}(t) &= \text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t) \\
\text{return\_margin}(t) &= \text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t)
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta x_{15m}(t) &= x(t) - x(t-1) \\
\text{run\_length}_x(t) &= j \times \text{direction} \\
\text{displacement}_x(t) &= \sum_{i=0}^{j-1} \Delta x_{15m}(t-i)
\end{aligned}$$

where $x \in \{ \text{humidity\_delta, supply\_margin, return\_margin} \}$ represents a given moisture gap, and $j$ represents the number of consecutive 15-minute intervals moving in the same continuous direction.

### 4.6 Summary of Engineered Features

The feature engineering phase transforms the raw sensor logs into a 24-dimensional geometric manifold. The complete feature set is summarized in the table below using standard mathematical notation.

| Category | Engineered Feature | Mathematical Definition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Power & Energy** | `dw_power`<br>`dw_energy` | $\text{power}(t) \times (\text{power}(t) - \text{power}(t-1))$<br>$\text{energy}(t) \times (\text{energy}(t) - \text{energy}(t-1))$ |
| **Outdoor Environment** | `d_rh_outdoor`<br>`d_t_outdoor` | $\text{rh\_outdoor}(t) - \text{rh\_outdoor}(t-1)$<br>$\text{t\_outdoor}(t) - \text{t\_outdoor}(t-1)$ |
| **Indoor Return Temp** | `d_t_return_15m`<br>`t_ret_run_length`<br>`t_ret_displacement` | $\text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_return}(t-1)$<br>$k \times \text{direction}$<br>$\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \Delta \text{t\_return}_{15m}(t-i)$ |
| **System Error & Thermal Effort** | `control_error`<br>`supply_delta`<br>`d_t_supply_15m`<br>`t_sup_run_length`<br>`t_sup_displacement` | $\text{t\_return}(t) - \text{sp\_return}(t)$<br>$\text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_return}(t)$<br>$\text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_supply}(t-1)$<br>$j \times \text{direction}$<br>$\sum_{i=0}^{j-1} \Delta \text{t\_supply}_{15m}(t-i)$ |
| **Moisture Gaps** | `humidity_delta`<br>`supply_margin`<br>`return_margin` | $\text{rh\_supply}(t) - \text{rh\_return}(t)$<br>$\text{t\_supply}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t)$<br>$\text{t\_return}(t) - \text{t\_saturation}(t)$ |
| **Moisture Kinematics** <br>*(Where $x$ is each of the 3 moisture gaps)* | `d_x_15m`<br>`run_length_x`<br>`displacement_x` | $x(t) - x(t-1)$<br>$m \times \text{direction}$<br>$\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} \Delta x_{15m}(t-i)$ |

### 4.7 Ranking Feature Contributions

A valuable aspect of the `isoRouting` workflow is its computational speed. We can take advantage of this efficiency to rank the individual contribution of each of the 24 engineered features to the upper tail of the anomaly score distribution ($S \ge 0.50$). Specifically, we evaluate 24 leave-one-out subsets of 23 features each and compare their upper-tail probability mass against the 24-feature baseline (`obs_tail_mass_50`), categorizing each feature as follows:

- **Positive contribution (Tail Driver):** If removing a feature causes the proportion of high anomaly scores to *drop* ($\mathbb{P}(S_{24} \ge 0.50) - \mathbb{P}(S_{-j} \ge 0.50) > 0$), that feature actively helps the forest isolate extreme behaviors.
- **Negative contribution (Diluter):** If removing a feature causes the proportion of high scores to *increase* ($\mathbb{P}(S_{24} \ge 0.50) - \mathbb{P}(S_{-j} \ge 0.50) < 0$), that feature tends to compress the separation between anomalous and normal scores.

```{r}
#| label: prep-feature-ranking
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Leave-One-Out Feature Ranking (24 Subsets of 23 Features)"

library(dplyr)
library(isotree)
library(parallel)

mat_24 <- as.matrix(df_comp[, vars_24])

# Fit a 500-tree forest on each of the 24 subsets of 23 features
feature_rank_df <- parallel::mclapply(seq_along(vars_24), function(j) {
  sub_mat_23 <- mat_24[, -j, drop = FALSE]
  
  iso_23 <- isolation.forest(
    sub_mat_23, ntrees = 500, sample_size = 256,
    nthreads = 1L, seed = 42, missing_action = "fail"
  )
  sc_23   <- predict(iso_23, sub_mat_23, nthreads = 1L)
  tail_23 <- mean(sc_23 >= 0.50)
  
  tibble(
    Feature      = vars_24[j],
    tail_mass_23 = tail_23,
    delta_tail   = obs_tail_mass_50 - tail_23,
    Effect       = ifelse(obs_tail_mass_50 >= tail_23, "Tail Driver (+)", "Diluter (-)")
  )
}, mc.cores = n_cores) |> bind_rows()

rm(mat_24)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-feature-ranking
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| code-summary: "Plot Code: Individual Feature Contributions to Upper-Tail Mass"
#| fig-cap: "Change in upper-tail probability mass (P(S >= 0.50)) when each of the 24 features is removed one at a time."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(feature_rank_df, aes(x = reorder(Feature, delta_tail), y = delta_tail, color = Effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = Feature, y = 0, yend = delta_tail), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Diluter (-)" = "#f8766d", "Tail Driver (+)" = "#00bfc4")) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual Feature Contributions to Upper-Tail Probability Mass",
    subtitle = sprintf("Baseline 24-feature tail mass P(S >= 0.50) = %.4f", obs_tail_mass_50),
    x = "Omitted Feature (23 Remaining)",
    y = expression(Delta ~ "Tail Probability Mass: " ~ P(S[24] >= 0.50) - P(S[-j] >= 0.50)),
    color = "Feature Role"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )
```

@fig-feature-ranking shows that 20 out of the 24 engineered features actively contribute to high anomaly scores in the baseline ensemble. This simple leave-one-out diagnostic illustrates how `isoRouting` can be used to quickly audit the marginal contribution of each candidate feature.

Next, we proceed with the full set of 24 engineered features to extract and route anomaly archetypes.

## 5 Archetype Extraction with Engineered Features

We now utilize the 24 engineered features to extract fault archetypes.

### 5.1 Engine Initialization

We initialize the engine with the engineered-feature YAML configuration and ingest the time course. To avoid scoring the 6-month summer gap as an anomaly, we split the data into `baseline_telemetry` and `stream_telemetry` using the `major_gap_idx` index calculated during [initial data validation](#data-split-and-validation).

```{r}
#| label: engine-init-and-split
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Initialize Engine and Split Data"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(isoRouting)

# 1. Load the package data and configure the engine
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")
config_engineered <- system.file(
  "extdata", "engineered_features.yaml",
  package = "isoRouting",
  mustWork = TRUE
)
engine_engineered <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_engineered)
engine_engineered <- ingest_time_course(engine_engineered, data = hvac_features)

# 2. Retrieve the validated telemetry mapped by the new YAML
hvac_valid_eng <- get_time_course(engine_engineered)

# 3. Bucket 1: Pre-Gap (~40% of data) for baseline archetype extraction
baseline_telemetry <- hvac_valid_eng |> 
  slice(1:major_gap_idx)

# 4. Bucket 2: Post-Gap (~60% of data) for predictive routing evaluation
stream_telemetry <- hvac_valid_eng |> 
  slice((major_gap_idx + 1):n())
```

### 5.2 Isolation Forest Training and Score Distribution

Next, we fit the Isolation Forest on `baseline_telemetry`. The engine pulls the ensemble size (`ntrees`: 500) and sample size (`sample_size`: 256) from the YAML configuration.

```{r}
#| label: fit-engineered-if
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Fit Isolation Forest"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)

# 1. Initialize a baseline-specific engine and ingest only the Winter 2019-2020 data
engine_baseline <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_engineered)
engine_baseline <- ingest_time_course(engine_baseline, data = baseline_telemetry)

# 2. Fit the Isolation Forest and extract anomalies 
engine_baseline <- extract_anomalies(engine_baseline)

# 3. Retrieve the scores for the entire baseline dataset
baseline_scores <- stats::predict(engine_baseline@model, engine_baseline@feature_matrix)

baseline_scored <- baseline_telemetry |>
  mutate(anomaly_score = baseline_scores)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-engineered-if-dist
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Score Distribution"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of Isolation Forest anomaly scores with the 24 engineered features."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(baseline_scored, aes(x = anomaly_score)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#4c72b0", color = "black", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Anomaly Score Distribution",
    subtitle = "Engineered features (Baseline: Winter 2019-2020)",
    x = "Anomaly Score",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

As shown in @fig-engineered-if-dist, most baseline observations fall below an anomaly score of 0.50, and the upper tail exhibits two distinct bumps around 0.52 and 0.65. As done with the naive configuration, we use `evaluate_k_stability` to explore anomaly thresholds by varying the number $N$ of top-scoring observations retained.

### 5.3 Threshold Diagnostics

We run `evaluate_k_stability` to compute the diagnostic profiles across candidate anomaly thresholds.

```{r}
#| label: engineered-evaluate-stability
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Run evaluate_k_stability"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Sweep based on size (N)
stability_curve_engineered <- evaluate_k_stability(
  engine_baseline, 
  max_N = 800, 
  min_N = 20, 
  nb_steps = 61, 
  max_k = 10
)
```

We then plot the profiles using the [previously defined wrapper](#stability-ggplot-target).

```{r}
#| label: fig-engineered-evaluate-stability
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic scores across anomaly thresholds (20 <= N <= 800)."
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-width: 7
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Generate the plot using the previously defined wrapper function
fig_engineered <- plot_topological_stability(
  stability_curve_engineered,
  plot_title = "Anomaly Threshold Diagnostics with Engineered Features",
  plot_subtitle = "Optimal cluster number (k), distance heterogeneity (D), and variable dependency breaks (LID)."
)

print(fig_engineered)
```

@fig-engineered-evaluate-stability shows that distance heterogeneity ($D$) peaks between thresholds $0.59$ and $0.61$. Within this interval, Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) remains elevated before beginning an overall decline.

As done with the naive configuration, we verify that the observed $D$ and LID values differ from random expectations by sampling sets of $N$ observations independently of their anomaly scores.

```{r}
#| label: engineered-null-preparation
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Simulate Engineered Controls"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Generate control quantiles using the engineered engine
lid_control_engineered <- simulate_lid_control(engine_baseline, N = n_sequence, iterations = 100)
dip_control_engineered <- simulate_dip_control(engine_baseline, N = n_sequence, iterations = 100)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-engineered-control-dip
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Simulated control bounds for Hartigan's D applied to the engineered feature matrix."

fig_dip_null_eng <- plot_baseline_profile(
  dip_control_engineered,
  line_color = "#009E73", 
  plot_title = "Engineered Control: Hartigan's D",
  plot_subtitle = "Expected distance heterogeneity.",
  y_label = "Hartigan's D"
)
print(fig_dip_null_eng)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-engineered-control-lid
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Simulated control bounds for LID applied to the engineered feature matrix."

fig_lid_null_eng <- plot_baseline_profile(
  lid_control_engineered,
  line_color = "#CC79A7", 
  plot_title = "Engineered Control: LID",
  plot_subtitle = "Expected structural dimensionality.",
  y_label = "LID"
)
print(fig_lid_null_eng)
```

In the engineered diagnostic profile (@fig-engineered-evaluate-stability), Hartigan's $D$ reaches approximately $0.045$ near $T = 0.60$, whereas the 95th percentile of the null control (@fig-engineered-control-dip) remains below $0.02$. This confirms that the observed multimodality reflects distinct anomaly states rather than an artifact of applying Hartigan's $D$ to pairwise distances.

The LID control (@fig-engineered-control-lid) provides similar confirmation: random subsets fluctuate between $20$ and $22$ dimensions (with a lower bound near $15$), whereas the anomaly subset drops from roughly $10.5$ to $8$ dimensions at $T = 0.60$.

Based on both diagnostics, we select $T = 0.60$ as the anomaly threshold.

### 5.4 Medoid Extraction

We now extract the cluster medoids (representative anomalies) at $T = 0.60$.

```{r}
#| label: extract-engineered-medoids
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Extract Archetypes at T = 0.6"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# 1. Isolate the top anomalies right after Hartigan's D peak
engine_baseline <- extract_medoids(engine_baseline, threshold = 0.6)

# 2. Retrieve the extracted physical archetypes (medoids)
medoids_df <- get_medoids(engine_baseline)

# 3. Print the calibrated k-value
cat("Calibrated k at threshold = 0.6:", engine_baseline@optimal_k, "\n")
```

At $T = 0.60$, maximizing the global silhouette score yields $k = 4$ clusters.

Next, we plot the trajectories of the four medoids using the [previously defined wrapper](#medoids-ggplot-target), displaying the `context_variables` specified in the YAML configuration.

```{r}
#| label: fig-engineered-comprehensive-medoids
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-cap: "Time course of the four anomaly archetypes extracted at T = 0.60."
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 8
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Retrieve the 10 context variables defined in the YAML
schema <- get_features(engine_baseline)
context_vars <- schema$context_variables

# Generate the plot
fig_medoids_comprehensive <- plot_medoid_trajectories(
  engine_baseline,
  plot_title = "Trajectories of the Four Archetypes at T = 0.6",
  plot_subtitle = "Trajectories of the context variables.",
  label_style = "numeric",
  vars_to_plot = context_vars
)

print(fig_medoids_comprehensive)
```

@fig-engineered-comprehensive-medoids reveals four distinct signatures:

* **Archetype 1:** Characterized by a dip in `t_supply` and a simultaneous spike in `rh_supply` at $t = 0$, while return variables, outdoor conditions, `sp_return`, `power`, and `energy` remain stable. This profile indicates a brief, unpowered moisture disturbance in the supply air.
* **Archetype 2:** Represents a system startup. At $t = 0$, `power` and `energy` step up sharply from near zero, accompanied by rising `t_supply` and `t_return` and falling `rh_supply` and `rh_return` as the air is heated without added moisture. Setpoint and outdoor variables remain constant.
* **Archetype 3:** Captures an unpowered thermal surge. At $t = 0$, `t_supply` spikes and remains elevated while `rh_supply` drops, yet `power` and `energy` stay near zero. This decoupling of thermal output from electrical input could reflect an external mechanical fault (such as a leaking heating valve).
* **Archetype 4:** Represents a system shutdown. At $t = 0$, `power` and `energy` drop to zero, initiating a steady decay in `t_supply` and `t_return` alongside a steady rise in `rh_supply` and `rh_return`, while outdoor conditions and the setpoint remain flat.

To quantify which features drive each archetype, `isoRouting` implements Leave-One-Covariate-Out (LOCO) ablation via method `ablate_features`. For each medoid, the method replaces one target variable at a time with its global median, recomputes the anomaly score, and ranks features by the resulting score drop.

```{r}
#| label: ablation-tests
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Run Ablation Tests"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

ablation_results <- ablate_features(engine_baseline)
```

```{r}
#| label: ablation-ggplot-function
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Define Ablation Plot Wrapper"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Reusable ablation plotting wrapper
plot_ablation_importance <- function(ablation_df, top_n = 5, plot_title, plot_subtitle) {
  
  # Filter to Top N drivers per cluster and retain raw variable names
  plot_data <- ablation_df |>
    group_by(cluster) |>
    slice_head(n = top_n) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(
      # Create a unique factor for faceted reordering using the raw variable name
      var_ordered = factor(paste(cluster, variable, sep = "__"))
    ) |>
    # Reorder based on the magnitude of the score drop
    mutate(var_ordered = reorder(var_ordered, score_drop))
  
  # Generate the plot
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = score_drop, y = var_ordered, fill = cluster)) +
    geom_col(color = "black", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.8) +
    facet_wrap(~cluster, scales = "free_y") +
    # Strip the cluster prefix to display just the raw variable name
    scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) gsub(".*__", "", x)) +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "turbo") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Anomaly Score Drop (Contribution Magnitude)",
      y = "Engineered Feature (Raw)"
    ) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
  
  return(p)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ablation-results
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-cap: "Top 5 engineered features driving the anomaly score for each medoid archetype, ranked by LOCO ablation."
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 10
#| warning: false
#| message: false

fig_ablation <- plot_ablation_importance(
  ablation_results, 
  top_n = 5,
  plot_title = "Medoid Interpretation via Feature Ablation",
  plot_subtitle = "Decrease in anomaly score when feature is reverted to its global median"
)

print(fig_ablation)
```

The LOCO ablation rankings (@fig-ablation-results) confirm the visual trajectory analysis:

* **Archetype 1:** Driven primarily by moisture features (`d_humidity_delta_15m` and `humidity_delta`), with no power features among the top contributors, confirming an unpowered moisture disturbance.
* **Archetype 2:** Led by `dw_power`, followed by thermal and energy step changes, consistent with a system startup.
* **Archetype 3:** Dominated by thermal step changes and saturation margins (`d_t_supply_15m`, `d_supply_margin_15m`) without power contributions, confirming an unpowered thermal fault.
* **Archetype 4:** Driven by shifts in saturation margins (`d_supply_margin_15m`, `displacement_return_margin`) and short-term temperature derivatives, matching a system shutdown.

### 5.5 Forensic Ledger

Once the cluster count is calibrated and medoids are extracted, we lock in the baseline using `commit_ledger()`. This method assigns every historical anomaly above the threshold to its nearest medoid based on Isolation Forest tree-assignment Hamming distance.

```{r}
#| label: commit-ledger
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Commit Baseline Ledger"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Lock the baseline and map all historical anomalies
engine_baseline <- commit_ledger(engine_baseline)

# Extract the flat dataframe for analysis
baseline_ledger <- get_ledger(engine_baseline)
head(baseline_ledger[, 1:4], 10)
```

Only the first four columns are shown above. `cluster_rank` orders anomalies by their distance to the cluster medoid (`1` denotes the medoid itself). The ledger also retains all target and context variables for every observation scoring above the threshold, enabling direct cluster summaries:

```{r}
#| label: ledger-summary
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Summarize Ledger"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

ledger_summary <- baseline_ledger |>
  group_by(anomaly_cluster) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Occurrences = n(),
    First_Seen        = min(as.Date(timestamp)),
    Last_Seen         = max(as.Date(timestamp)),
    Median_Score      = round(median(anomaly_score), 3),
    Max_Distance      = round(max(topological_distance), 3)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(Total_Occurrences))

kable(ledger_summary, caption = "Summary of historical anomaly archetypes.")
```

`Max_Distance` defines the **radius** of each cluster—the maximum forest distance between its medoid (`topological_distance = 0`) and its members. Later, we use these cluster radii to route sub-threshold observations and flag novel anomaly types in new data.

First, we examine the cumulative occurrence of each archetype over time at $T = 0.60$.

```{r}
#| label: cumulative-faults
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Cumulative Archetype Occurrences"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(dplyr)

cumulative_ledger <- baseline_ledger |>
  arrange(timestamp) |>
  group_by(anomaly_cluster) |>
  mutate(cumulative_count = row_number()) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cumulative-faults
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative frequency of the four fault archetypes across the baseline period."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)

plot_data <- cumulative_ledger |>
  arrange(anomaly_cluster == "Cluster 4", timestamp)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = timestamp, y = cumulative_count, color = anomaly_cluster)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.9) + # Ensures single-occurrence events are visible
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title    = "Cumulative Frequency of Fault Archetypes (Baseline Period)",
    subtitle = "Accelerating curves would indicate progressive mechanical degradation",
    x        = "Timeline",
    y        = "Cumulative Occurrences",
    color    = "Archetype"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

This cumulative profile tests for progressive wear-and-tear faults, which would manifest as upward-curving trajectories (an increasing occurrence rate over time). @fig-cumulative-faults shows no progressive degradation:

* **Cluster 4:** Occurs once in January, consistent with an isolated system shutdown.
* **Cluster 1:** Appears only during autumn and flatlines by December, pointing to a seasonal moisture disturbance.
* **Cluster 3:** Accumulates primarily during the coldest winter months, matching its signature of unpowered `t_supply` surges.
* **Cluster 2:** The most frequent archetype, steepening during peak winter (December through February) before tapering off in spring.

To investigate why Cluster 2 accumulates steadily during winter, we plot archetype occurrences by both date and time of day.

```{r}
#| label: date-time-scatter
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Extract Date and Time of Day"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(hms)

scatter_data <- baseline_ledger |>
  mutate(
    date        = as.Date(timestamp),
    time_of_day = as_hms(timestamp)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-date-time-scatter
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| fig-cap: "Occurrence dates and times of day for each fault archetype."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(scatter_data, aes(x = date, y = time_of_day, color = anomaly_cluster)) +
  # Map size to distance. Smaller distance = larger point (closer to medoid)
  geom_point(aes(size = topological_distance), alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    trans = "reverse", 
    range = c(1, 6),
    name  = "Topological Distance\n(Larger = closer to medoid)"
  ) +
  scale_y_time(breaks = scales::breaks_width("4 hours")) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo", guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~anomaly_cluster, ncol = 2) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title    = "Dates and Times of Archetypes",
    subtitle = "Y-axis isolates time of day; Point size reflects proximity to the medoid",
    x        = "Date",
    y        = "Time of Day"
  ) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

@fig-date-time-scatter clarifies the operational context of each cluster:

* **Cluster 2:** Occurs strictly around 5:00 AM. Its winter steepening reflects the morning heating demand required to bring a cold building up to setpoint.
* **Cluster 1:** Also clusters in the early morning hours, but only during autumn. This aligns with morning startups coinciding with autumn humidity and dew-point swings before drier winter air arrives.
* **Cluster 3:** Occurs across the day (around 7:00 AM, 2:00 PM, and 4:00 PM). This lack of schedule dependence fits a mechanical issue—such as a leaking heating valve or damper—triggered by varying thermal loads.
* **Cluster 4:** Appears once in the late afternoon, consistent with an isolated shutdown or manual override outside routine morning transitions.

Next, we use the cluster radii to examine lower-scoring anomalies.

### 5.6 Sub-Threshold Anomaly Tracking via Cluster Radii

Analyzing only observations above $T = 0.60$ focuses on severe fault manifestations, whereas early precursors or gradual mechanical wear may develop below that cutoff. To track sub-threshold behavior, we use the cluster radii (`Max_Distance`) established at $T = 0.60$ as filters. 

The `route_time_course()` method computes the forest Hamming distance between every observation in the scored time course (`get_scored_time_course()`) and each medoid. Any observation falling within a cluster's radius is assigned to that archetype regardless of its anomaly score, while observations outside all four radii are labeled `"Background"`.

```{r}
#| label: routed-timeline
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Route Full Time Course"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(dplyr)

# Route the full time course using cluster radii
routed_timeline <- route_time_course(engine_baseline)
print(table(routed_timeline$archetype_bucket))

# Retain all observations assigned to the fault archetypes
routed_archetypes <- subset(routed_timeline, archetype_bucket != "Background")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-routed-timeline
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Temporal evolution of anomaly scores for all observations falling within each archetype's cluster radius. The red dashed line marks the T = 0.60 threshold; solid black lines and grey bands represent Generalized Additive Model (GAM) smoothers and their 95% confidence intervals."

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(routed_archetypes, aes(x = timestamp, y = anomaly_score, color = archetype_bucket)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"), 
    color = "black", linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.6, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~archetype_bucket, ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo", guide = "none") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title    = "Temporal Evolution of Archetype Anomaly Scores",
    subtitle = "Archetypes bounded by their maximum baseline forest distance (cluster radius)",
    x        = "Timeline",
    y        = "Anomaly Score"
  ) +
  theme(strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0"))
```

@fig-routed-timeline plots all baseline observations captured within each medoid's radius (excluding `"Background"` points). The red dashed line marks the $T = 0.60$ extraction cutoff, while the black curves and grey bands show Generalized Additive Model (GAM) cubic regression spline trends and their 95% confidence intervals.

This view captures system behavior across both high- and low-score regimes without altering the cluster definitions:

* **Effect of a Higher Threshold ($T > 0.60$):** Above $T = 0.64$, Cluster 1 (peaking below $0.64$) and Cluster 4 ($0.605$) disappear, leaving only the extreme tails of Clusters 2 and 3.
* **Cluster 1:** Exhibits a tight band of sub-threshold precursors (scores between $0.49$ and $0.60$) during the same autumn window as its above-threshold points, with a flat mean trend near $0.585$.
* **Cluster 2:** Follows a seasonal arch. Mild occurrences ($0.50\text{--}0.58$) appear in November before the GAM trend crosses $0.60$ in December, plateaus near $0.64$ during peak winter heating (January–February), and subsides in spring. Because the trend declines as outdoor temperatures warm, it reflects seasonal heating load rather than progressive wear.
* **Cluster 3:** Most observations sharing this unpowered thermal-surge signature sit below $0.60$. Its GAM trend remains below the cutoff all winter (drifting from $0.55$ down to $0.52$ by April), confirming that the fault does not worsen over time.
* **Cluster 4:** Because this singleton cluster has a radius of $0$, no sub-threshold observations fall within its boundary and no trend curve is fitted.

## 6 Predictive Routing and Novelty Detection on Streaming Telemetry

Once the baseline archetypes and their cluster radii (`@cluster_radii`) are locked inside `engine_baseline`, the `DiagnosticEngine` can route new observations without retraining the Isolation Forest or re-running hierarchical clustering.

When new data arrive, `predict_stream()` projects each observation through the frozen baseline forest (`@model`), extracts its terminal leaf-node signature (`type = "tree_num"`), and computes its proportional Hamming distance to each cached medoid signature (`@baseline_signatures`). Each observation is then classified by combining **forest distance** and **anomaly score**:

1. **Known Fault Archetype (`Cluster 1` ... `Cluster k`):** The observation's Hamming distance to its nearest medoid falls within that cluster's baseline radius ($d \le R_c$).
2. **Background (`Background`):** The observation falls outside all cluster radii ($d > R_c$) and its anomaly score remains below the baseline threshold ($S < 0.60$).
3. **Novel Anomaly (`Novel Anomaly`):** The observation exceeds the anomaly score threshold ($S \ge 0.60$) **and** falls outside the radius of every known medoid ($d > R_c$). This flags an unseen fault mode that did not occur during the baseline period.

### 6.1 Routing the Incoming Stream

```{r}
#| label: predict-stream
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Route and Summarize Streaming Telemetry"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(dplyr)

# Route unseen streaming telemetry using the locked baseline engine
stream_routed <- predict_stream(engine_baseline, new_data = stream_telemetry)

# Lookup vector of baseline cluster radii (returns NA for Background and Novel Anomaly)
radii_lookup <- engine_baseline@cluster_radii

# Summarize the routed states
stream_summary <- stream_routed |>
  group_by(predicted_state) |>
  summarise(
    Occurrences     = n(),
    Median_Score    = round(median(anomaly_score, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Max_Score       = round(max(anomaly_score, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Median_Distance = round(median(distance_to_archetype, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Cluster_Radius  = round(unname(radii_lookup[first(predicted_state)]), 3),
    .groups         = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(Occurrences))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predict-stream
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Table Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(knitr)

kable(
  stream_summary,
  caption = "Summary of streaming telemetry routed across baseline archetypes and novelty bounds."
)
```

@tbl-predict-stream summarizes the classification of the $16,634$ post-gap streaming observations:

* **Background** ($16,451$ occurrences): Nearly $98.9\%$ of the incoming stream remains below $T = 0.60$ (maximum score $0.599$) and sits outside the baseline cluster radii (median Hamming distance $0.914$).
* **Known Archetypes** (`Cluster 2`, `Cluster 3`, `Cluster 1`): A total of $166$ observations fall within the radius ($d \le R_c$) of an established medoid. Consistent with the winter baseline period, `Cluster 2` (morning heating startup) dominates with $114$ occurrences, followed by `Cluster 3` (unpowered thermal surge, $49$ occurrences) and `Cluster 1` (autumn moisture disturbance, $3$ occurrences). Because routing uses cluster radii rather than a score cutoff, `predict_stream()` also captures sub-threshold occurrences of known faults (such as `Cluster 3` with a median score of $0.549$). `Cluster 4` records zero matches because its baseline singleton radius is $R_4 = 0$.
* **Novel Anomaly** ($17$ occurrences): Seventeen observations exceed $T = 0.60$ (median score $0.643$, maximum $0.684$) while falling outside the radius of every baseline medoid (median distance $0.746$).

### 6.2 Isolating and Clustering Novel Anomalies

Rather than pooling historical and streaming anomalies together—which allows frequent faults like `Cluster 2` to dominate the distance matrix—we keep the locked baseline archetypes and pass `stream_routed` directly to method `isolate_novel_anomalies()`.

This method branches `engine_baseline` onto the $17$ `Novel Anomaly` observations, computes their pairwise Hamming distances using the frozen baseline forest, selects the optimal number of novel sub-clusters via DIANA and global silhouette width, extracts their $\pm 2$-hour medoid windows, and commits a dedicated ledger.

```{r}
#| label: isolate-novel-anomalies
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Isolate and Summarize Novel Anomalies"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(dplyr)

# Branch a novel DiagnosticEngine onto the 17 Novel Anomaly observations
engine_novel <- isolate_novel_anomalies(engine_baseline, stream_routed, min_k = 2, max_k = 6)

# Inspect the global silhouette profile across k = 2..6
print(engine_novel@k_metrics)

# Extract and summarize the novel forensic ledger
novel_ledger <- get_ledger(engine_novel)

novel_summary <- novel_ledger |>
  group_by(anomaly_cluster) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Occurrences = n(),
    First_Seen        = min(as.Date(timestamp)),
    Last_Seen         = max(as.Date(timestamp)),
    Median_Score      = round(median(anomaly_score), 3),
    Max_Distance      = round(max(topological_distance), 3),
    .groups           = "drop"
  )
```

Evaluating the global silhouette width across $k \in [2, 6]$ identifies a peak at $k = 4$ ($\text{Global Silhouette} = 0.527$), partitioning the $17$ novel events into four sub-clusters. Because `engine_novel` is a standard `DiagnosticEngine` object, we summarize its ledger using `get_ledger()`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-novel-subclusters
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Table Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(knitr)

kable(
  novel_summary,
  caption = "Summary of the 17 novel anomalies partitioned into k = 4 DIANA sub-clusters (Global Silhouette = 0.527)."
)
```

@tbl-novel-subclusters shows a clear seasonal split across the four novel sub-clusters:

* **Late-Autumn Modes** (`Cluster_1` and `Cluster_2`): Both occur within a five-day window in late November 2020 (`2020-11-23` to `2020-11-27`), with $6$ and $3$ occurrences, respectively.
* **Late-Winter Modes** (`Cluster_3` and `Cluster_4`): Both emerge between late February and mid-March 2021 (`2021-02-27` to `2021-03-19`), with $6$ occurrences in `Cluster_3` (median score $0.664$) and $2$ occurrences in `Cluster_4` (`2021-03-13` to `2021-03-17`).

### 6.3 Trajectories and Feature Ablation of Novel Archetypes

Because `engine_novel` stores the extracted $\pm 2$-hour medoid windows and baseline feature matrix, we pass it directly to the previously defined [medoid plotting wrapper](#medoids-ggplot-target).

```{r}
#| label: prep-novel-medoids-trajectories
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Data Preparation: Extract Context Variables for Novel Medoids"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

context_vars <- get_features(engine_novel)$context_variables
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-novel-medoids-trajectories
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-cap: "Time-course trajectories of the context variables for the four novel anomaly sub-clusters extracted from the streaming telemetry."

fig_novel_medoids <- plot_medoid_trajectories(
  engine_novel,
  plot_title    = "Trajectories of the Four Novel Sub-Clusters (Streaming Telemetry)",
  plot_subtitle = "Trajectories of the context variables across +/- 2 hour windows.",
  label_style   = "numeric",
  vars_to_plot  = context_vars
)

print(fig_novel_medoids)
```

@fig-novel-medoids-trajectories shows how the four novel sub-clusters compare to the baseline archetypes:

* **Novel Archetype 1 ($n = 6$):** Exhibits a one-hour surge in `power` ($0 \to 5\text{ kW}$) and `energy` accompanied by opposing temperature shifts. Unlike a normal heating cycle, `t_supply` dips from $30^\circ\text{C}$ to $24^\circ\text{C}$ (with a spike in `rh_supply`) while `t_return` rises from $18^\circ\text{C}$ to $21^\circ\text{C}$ before reverting when power returns to zero.
* **Novel Archetype 2 ($n = 3$):** Resembles Baseline Archetype 3 in that `t_supply` surges from $17^\circ\text{C}$ to $30^\circ\text{C}$ (driving `rh_supply` down from $45\%$ to $30\%$) while `power` and `energy` remain near zero. Here, however, the surge is sustained and followed by oscillations in `t_saturation` ($17^\circ\text{C}\text{--}21^\circ\text{C}$).
* **Novel Archetypes 3 ($n = 6$) and 4 ($n = 2$):** Both show a sustained step-up in `power` ($0 \to 5\text{ kW}$) and `energy` at $t = 0$, similar to Baseline Archetype 2. However, whereas Baseline Archetype 2 drove simultaneous increases in `t_supply` and `t_return`, here `t_supply` and `t_saturation` drop at $t = 0$—sharply in Novel Archetype 3 (`sp_return` $\approx 19.5^\circ\text{C}$, with `t_saturation` falling from $19^\circ\text{C}$ to $14^\circ\text{C}$) and more moderately in Novel Archetype 4 (`sp_return` $\approx 21.5^\circ\text{C}$, preceded by a ramp in `rh_return`).

To identify the engineered features separating these four novel fault modes—particularly Novel Archetypes 3 and 4—we run `ablate_features()` on `engine_novel`.

```{r}
#| label: prep-novel-ablation
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: show
#| code-summary: "Run LOCO Ablation on Novel Medoids"
#| message: false
#| warning: false

novel_ablation_results <- ablate_features(engine_novel)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-novel-ablation
#| echo: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-cap: "Top 5 engineered features driving the anomaly score for each novel sub-cluster medoid, ranked by LOCO ablation."

fig_novel_ablation <- plot_ablation_importance(
  novel_ablation_results,
  top_n         = 5,
  plot_title    = "Novel Sub-Cluster Interpretation via Feature Ablation",
  plot_subtitle = "Decrease in anomaly score when feature is reverted to its baseline median"
)

print(fig_novel_ablation)
```

The LOCO ablation results (@fig-novel-ablation) clarify the feature drivers behind each novel sub-cluster:

* **Novel Cluster 1:** Driven by rapid changes in return temperature (`d_t_return_15m`) and humidity (`d_humidity_delta_15m`) coupled with power and energy (`dw_power`, `dw_energy`). Whereas Baseline Archetype 1 was an unpowered moisture disturbance, this fault pairs a moisture and return-air transient with a brief power pulse.
* **Novel Cluster 2:** Contains no power or energy features among its top five drivers. Unlike Baseline Archetype 3—which was driven by 15-minute thermal step changes—Novel Cluster 2 is dominated by cumulative multi-step displacements (`displacement_supply_margin`, `t_sup_displacement`, `displacement_humidity_delta`), capturing the sustained thermal ramp and saturation instability.
* **Novel Cluster 3 vs. Novel Cluster 4:** Although both are led by `dw_power` (and include `dw_energy`), their secondary drivers explain why DIANA separates them:
  * **Novel Cluster 3** is driven by **return-saturation margins**: ranks 2, 3, and 4 consist of `d_return_margin_15m`, `displacement_return_margin`, and `return_margin`, reflecting the $5^\circ\text{C}$ drop in `t_saturation` relative to `t_return` at startup.
  * **Novel Cluster 4** is driven by **humidity-delta kinematics** (`d_humidity_delta_15m` at rank 2 and `run_length_humidity_delta` at rank 5) alongside `d_return_margin_15m` (rank 3), capturing the two-hour climb in `rh_return` ($18\% \to 27\%$) relative to `rh_supply` prior to the power surge.

Combining the trajectory profiles (@fig-novel-medoids-trajectories) with the LOCO feature rankings (@fig-novel-ablation) suggests the following physical interpretations for the four novel fault modes:

- **Novel Cluster 1 (Economizer or Outdoor-Air Damper Transient):** A one-hour `power` pulse occurs alongside a drop in `t_supply` ($30^\circ\text{C} \to 24^\circ\text{C}$) and a rise in `t_return` ($18^\circ\text{C} \to 21^\circ\text{C}$). This pattern might represent an economizer or outdoor-air damper opening in response to rising indoor return temperatures (`d_t_return_15m`), drawing in cooler, more humid autumn air (`d_humidity_delta_15m`) while the supply fan powers up to flush the zone.
- **Novel Cluster 2 (Sustained Heating Valve Leak):** Whereas Baseline Archetype 3 captured brief unpowered thermal spikes, Novel Cluster 2 could reflect a heating coil valve stuck partially open over multiple hours. In this scenario, hot water continues to heat the supply air (`t_sup_displacement`, `displacement_supply_margin`) while electrical `power` remains off, triggering downstream oscillations in `t_saturation`.
- **Novel Cluster 3 (Mechanical Cooling or Defrost Engagement):** A sharp `power` step-up is paired with an immediate drop in both `t_supply` and `t_saturation` ($19^\circ\text{C} \to 14^\circ\text{C}$) at a lower return setpoint (`sp_return` $\approx 19.5^\circ\text{C}$). Rather than a winter heating startup (Baseline Archetype 2), this could reflect compressor-driven cooling or a heat-pump defrost cycle that rapidly chills the coil below the return-air temperature (`d_return_margin_15m`, `displacement_return_margin`).
- **Novel Cluster 4 (Latent Occupancy Load / Dehumidification Startup):** Preceded by a steady two-hour climb in `rh_return` ($18\% \to 27\%$) at a higher setpoint (`sp_return` $\approx 21.5^\circ\text{C}$), the unit powers on (`dw_power`), likely to address accumulated indoor moisture (`d_humidity_delta_15m`, `run_length_humidity_delta`), producing a milder drop in `t_supply` and `t_saturation` as moisture condenses across the coil.

## 7 Turin HVAC Case Study: Key Findings

Applying the `isoRouting` pipeline to the Turin HVAC telemetry dataset demonstrated how an unsupervised Isolation Forest can be turned into an interpretable, end-to-end fault routing system. Across the pre-gap baseline and post-gap streaming periods, the analysis yielded four main findings:

- **Feature Dilution vs. Signal Drivers:** Adding 6 mode-dwell counters to the 24 thermodynamic and control features compressed the upper tail of the anomaly score distribution rather than sharpening it (@fig-score-compression-24-vs-30, @fig-mc-feature-subset-control). A subsequent leave-one-out audit confirmed that 20 of the 24 retained features actively drive high anomaly scores (@fig-feature-ranking). Because forest scoring is fast and `DiagnosticEngine` decouples feature selection into external YAML files, auditing and swapping feature sets required no changes to the downstream pipeline.
- **Validated Multimodal Fault Regimes:** On the pre-gap baseline telemetry, varying candidate anomaly thresholds revealed a clear operating regime where extracted anomalies separated into $k = 4$ distinct, low-dimensional clusters. `evaluate_k_stability()` (@fig-engineered-evaluate-stability) alongside the Monte Carlo null controls in `simulate_dip_control()` (@fig-engineered-control-dip) and `simulate_lid_control()` (@fig-engineered-control-lid) provided quantitative bounds to select both the score cutoff and the number of baseline clusters ($k$).
- **Interpretable Physical Archetypes:** Partitioning the baseline tail by leaf-sharing Hamming distance summarized thousands of timestamps into a compact set of concrete historical trajectories (`extract_medoids()`, @fig-engineered-comprehensive-medoids) logged via `commit_ledger()`. Leave-One-Covariate-Out ablation (`ablate_features()`, @fig-ablation-results) linked each archetype directly to its driving physical channels—such as supply/return temperature displacements and control margins—turning abstract anomaly scores into actionable root-cause profiles.
- **Precursor Tracking and Emerging Post-Gap Faults:** Caching the baseline medoid signatures (`@baseline_signatures`) and cluster radii (`@cluster_radii`) enabled immediate classification of additional telemetry without retraining the forest. `route_time_course()` revealed sub-threshold precursors leading into major events (@fig-routed-timeline), while `predict_stream()` triaged post-gap telemetry into normal operation, recurring baseline archetypes, and out-of-distribution events (@tbl-predict-stream). Branching a secondary engine onto the rejected events via `isolate_novel_anomalies()` showed that the post-gap novelties were four new emerging fault regimes (@tbl-novel-subclusters, @fig-novel-medoids-trajectories, @fig-novel-ablation).
